pages.content:
Introduction
Binghamton University’s graduate admissions process includes several additional steps for international students. These steps are designed to satisfy U.S. immigration and visa requirements and to ensure that applicants have the financial resources to complete their studies.

Application Materials
1. Passport
Applicants must upload a scan of the passport page that shows their name, citizenship, and date of birth. Providing this page early can speed the issuance of the I‑20 or DS‑2019 form.
2. International Student Financial Statement (ISFS)
The ISFS is a form that attests the applicant has sufficient funds for tuition, fees, and living expenses for at least one year of graduate study. Even if the applicant receives university funding, the ISFS must still be submitted.
3. Supporting Financial Documentation
In addition to the ISFS, applicants must provide documents that support the funding sources listed on the ISFS. Common documents include official bank statements, scholarship or sponsorship letters, or a university funding offer letter. If the university’s funding offer is less than the amount certified on the ISFS, additional documentation is required.
4. Proof of English Proficiency
International applicants must submit scores from one of the following tests: TOEFL iBT, TOEFL Essentials, IELTS, Pearson PTE Academic, or Duolingo English Test. Scores should be sent electronically by the testing agency to Binghamton’s Graduate Admissions Office using the university’s code (e.g., 2535 for TOEFL). Some programs may require higher minimum scores.

English Proficiency Waivers
Waivers are available for applicants who meet any of the following criteria at the time of enrollment:
• Citizen or permanent resident of a waiver‑eligible country where English is the official language and the medium of instruction.
• Holds or has earned a bachelor’s degree or higher from an institution in a waiver‑eligible country.
• Completed at least two years of full‑time study at an accredited institution in a waiver‑eligible country.
The list of waiver‑eligible countries includes the United States, United Kingdom (England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales), Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Ghana, Liberia, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Botswana, Zambia, Malawi, Gambia, Tanzania, and some Canadian provinces. Applicants who qualify should contact the Graduate Admissions Office to obtain a waiver.

Funding and Assistantships
University funding is still required to be documented via the ISFS. Graduate assistantships are competitive and awarded based on academic merit. No additional materials are required for assistantship consideration unless a specific program states otherwise.

Submission Tips
Uploading all required documents during the application process can expedite the issuance of immigration documents. However, documents are not mandatory for the initial application; they can be submitted after an admission decision if the applicant relies on program funding.

Known Eligibility
• Visa types: F‑1 or J‑1.
• Must provide passport page, ISFS, supporting financial docs, and English proficiency scores.
• Waiver eligibility depends on citizenship, education, and study history in specified countries.

Funding
• University funding still requires ISFS.
• Graduate assistantships are merit‑based; no extra materials unless specified.

Deadline
The source text does not specify a universal application deadline. Individual programs may have distinct deadlines.

Unknowns
• Exact list of acceptable financial documents beyond bank statements and scholarship letters.
• Full list of waiver‑eligible Canadian provinces.
• Program‑specific minimum English proficiency scores.

Source Limitations

pages.content:
Overview
Nearly half of graduate students at the University of Alabama receive some form of funding. Funding is limited to students who have been admitted to a degree‑seeking program and who have completed an undergraduate degree at enrollment.

Eligibility
- General eligibility: admission to a degree‑seeking graduate program and completion of an undergraduate degree.
- Assistantships (GTA, GRA, GA): Open to most graduate students; international students in GTAs must complete the International Teaching Assistant Program. English Language Institute students cannot hold internally funded assistantships.
- Graduate School Fellowships: Must be nominated by the student's department; nominees must be admitted students.
- Capstone Doctoral Fellowship (CDF): Requires a five‑year funding package; awards made before Jan 15 2027.
- Graduate Council and National Alumni Association Fellowships: Open to full‑time on‑campus students who are Alabama residents. Nomination deadlines are Dec 10 2026 (students graduating fall/summer 2028), Jan 14 2027 (new students starting summer/fall 2027), and Feb 11 2027 (new students starting summer/fall 2027).
- Strategic Graduate Partnerships Initiative (SGPI) Fellowships: Must be full‑time on‑campus students; eligibility includes a bachelor’s degree from an SGPI partner or completion of an SGPI Summer REU. Deadline is the Monday immediately after UA Spring Break (date not specified).
- Joint Faculty Development Program Fellowships: Available to faculty at partner institutions without terminal degrees; no listed deadline.
- SREB Doctoral Scholars Program: Open to newly admitted doctoral students planning a teaching career; provides a $20,000 stipend and tuition scholarship.
- Fulbright Tuition Scholarships: Provide a 100 % tuition scholarship for Fulbright awardees.
- Alumni Heritage Graduate Scholarship: One‑time $500 award for Alabama‑resident first‑semester graduate students who are children or grandchildren of UA alumni meeting specific membership criteria.

Funding Types
- Assistantships: Include a stipend, tuition scholarship (up to 15 credit hours or actual tuition, whichever is less), fee coverage, and single‑coverage health insurance. Partial assistantships cover only a portion of these costs.
- Fellowships: Vary by program; CDF offers at least $35,000 annual stipend plus tuition and fees. Graduate Council/National Alumni Fellowships provide $20,000–$25,000 stipends and full tuition, health insurance, and fee coverage.
- Scholarships: Listed under Graduate School Scholarships and other external sources (e.g., NSF GRFP, DOE, Jacob Javits, Fulbright). Effects on federal aid should be checked with the Office of Student Financial Aid.
- On‑Campus Employment: Hourly jobs up to 20 hours/week during the academic year (40 hours in summer).
- Conference and Research Funding: Grants up to $500–$800 for conferences and $300–$600 for research, matched by departments. Priority funding cycles run Sep 1 2025–Feb 28 2026, Dec 1 2025–May 30 2026, Mar 1 2026–Aug 30 2026, Jun 1 2026–Nov 30 2026.

pages.content:
Introduction
This article synthesizes information from a Kaplan Test Prep guide (April 2021) to outline common steps, eligibility factors, funding sources, and deadlines for graduate‑school applications. The source is treated as unverified and may not reflect current policies.

Application Timeline
- 2 years before enrollment: Begin researching fields, programs, and potential advisors.
- 1 year before: Prepare for and take the GRE, start assembling transcripts, resumes, and letters of recommendation, and explore financial‑aid options.
- 9 months before: Application portals typically open; submit applications as early as possible.
- 6 months before: Review admission offers, compare programs, and decide where to matriculate.

Eligibility Requirements (Typical, not exhaustive)
- Undergraduate cumulative GPA (often required; exact minimum varies by program).
- GRE scores (required by many programs; specific score thresholds are program‑specific and not provided in the source).
- Letters of recommendation (usually 2–3, requested early).
- Personal statement or statement of purpose.
- Some programs may require an interview, a portfolio, or additional tests (e.g., GMAT, LSAT).

GRE Score Considerations
The guide notes that GRE scores are used alongside GPA to assess readiness. It advises checking each program’s published average or minimum scores, if available, and contacting admissions offices when data are missing. No universal “good” score is defined.

Choosing a Program
Factors highlighted include location, cost, reputation, curriculum fit, career services, and school culture. Prospective students are encouraged to review program websites, attend open houses, and speak with faculty or current students. The guide does not provide quantitative rankings.

Funding Options
- FAFSA: Primary federal aid application for graduate students; does not require parental information.
- Merit‑based aid: Scholarships, fellowships, teaching or research assistantships that may cover tuition and provide stipends.
- Military benefits: Post‑9/11 GI Bill and Yellow Ribbon programs for eligible veterans or spouses.
- Employer tuition‑reimbursement programs (subject to employer policies).
- Faith‑based and non‑traditional scholarships (e.g., for students over 25).
- Personal financing: IRA loans, home‑equity loans, or private loans (not recommended without careful consideration).

Deadlines and Planning
The guide stresses that each program sets its own deadline, generally in the fall or winter preceding the intended start term. Early submission is recommended to avoid missing deadlines for both admission and financial‑aid applications.

Unknowns and Source Limitations
- Exact GPA or GRE cut‑offs for specific programs are not provided.
- Funding amounts, availability of assistantships, and scholarship eligibility criteria vary widely and are not detailed.
- The guide’s publication date (2021) means policies may have changed (e.g., test‑optional trends, pandemic‑related adjustments).
- No data on acceptance rates, post‑graduation salaries, or program‑specific outcomes are included.

Conclusion
While the Kaplan guide offers a useful high‑level roadmap, prospective applicants should verify current requirements and deadlines directly with each graduate program and consult up‑to‑date financial‑aid resources.

pages.content:
# Overview
Graduate fellowships at UW‑Madison provide financial support and professional development for students pursuing advanced degrees. Fellowships can be awarded by the university, external agencies, professional societies, or private foundations. They typically require sustained progress in research and completion of degree requirements.

# University‑Funded Fellowships
- **Funding Forward**: A program that equips students to apply for external fellowships. It offers workshops, writing groups, and one‑on‑one consultations. No stipend is provided directly; it supports the application process.
- **Hoodie Incentive**: Students who apply for certain external fellowships during the 2025‑26 academic year may receive a free UW‑Madison hoodie. Eligible fellowships include ACLS Robert H. N. Ho Family Foundation, BTAA/Smithsonian, Charlotte W. Newcombe, Ford Foundation, FINESST, Hertz, HHMI Gilliam, Mellon/ACLS, National GEM Consortium, National Physical Science Consortium, NSF GRFP, NIH Training Grants, Robert Wood Johnson Health Policy Research Scholars, Rome Prize, SSRC, Spencer, NSERC, DOE Computational Science Graduate Fellowship, and others.

# External Fellowships
| Fellowship | Eligibility | Stipend / Tuition | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP)** | U.S. citizens or permanent residents | $37,000 annual stipend + $16,000 tuition assistance (3 years) | Requires sustained progress in science/engineering research. |
| **Fulbright‑Hays Doctoral Research Fellowship** | U.S. citizen, national, or permanent resident | Not specified in source | Supports study, teaching, or research abroad. |
| **HHMI Gilliam Fellowships** | Second or third‑year biomedical or life‑science PhD students and their advisors | Not specified | Focus on mentorship and professional development. |
| **Hertz Fellowship** | College seniors or first‑year graduate students; U.S. citizens or permanent residents | Not specified | Emphasizes inclusive research methodologies. |
| **Spencer Dissertation Fellowship (NAEd/Spencer)** | PhD students who have completed pre‑dissertation requirements | Stipend + professional development retreats | Supports final dissertation analysis and writing. |
| **Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship** | Doctoral students in humanities or interpretive social sciences; encourages underrepresented groups | Stipend + funding for research, travel, mentorship | Supports innovative dissertation projects. |
| **DOE Office of Science Graduate Student Research Program (SCGSR)** | Graduate students eligible for DOE lab research | Not specified | Provides thesis research opportunities at DOE laboratories. |
| **HHMI Gilliam Fellowships** | Second or third‑year biomedical or life‑science PhD students and their advisors | Not specified | Focus on mentorship and professional development. |
| **Hertz Fellowship** | College seniors or first‑year graduate students; U.S. citizens or permanent residents | Not specified | Emphasizes inclusive research and innovative methodologies. |
| **Spencer Dissertation Fellowship** | PhD students who have completed all pre‑dissertation requirements | Stipend + professional development | Supports final dissertation writing. |
| **Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship** | Doctoral students in humanities or interpretive social sciences | Stipend + additional funding for research, travel, mentorship | Encourages applications from historically underrepresented groups. |
| **DOE SCGSR** | Graduate students with access to DOE laboratories | Not specified | Supports thesis research at DOE labs. |

# Resources for Grant‑Seeking
- **Funding Forward**: Workshops and micro‑courses on grant writing.
- **Micro‑Course: Grants & Funding**: Introductory course covering planning, researching, writing, and follow‑up.
- **Grants Information Collection (GIC)**: Databases, guides, and directories for identifying grants and fellowships.
- **Wisconsin Scholarship Hub (WiSH)**: Search portal for scholarships, grants, and fellowships specific to UW‑Madison students.
- **International Fellowships Office (IRIS Awards Office)**: Coordinates international research and study‑abroad funding.
- **Fulbright U.S. Student Program**: Campus coordinator assists in matching opportunities.
- **Pivot, Fastweb, Fastweb, Modern Language Association (MLA) Fellowships & Grants List**: External platforms that list additional opportunities; contact the UW‑Madison Associate Director of Graduate Funding for interpretation.

# Eligibility & Funding Summary
- **Citizenship**: Most external fellowships require U.S. citizenship or permanent residency. Some (e.g., NSF GRFP, Hertz, Spencer) explicitly state this.
- **Degree Stage**: Fellowships vary from undergraduate seniors to first‑year graduate students to post‑doctoral researchers. For example, Hertz targets college seniors and first‑year grad students; HHMI Gilliam targets second/third‑year PhD students.
- **Discipline**: Some fellowships are discipline‑specific (e.g., Mellon/ACLS for humanities/social sciences, Spencer for education research, DOE SCGSR for STEM). Others are broad (NSF GRFP, Fulbright‑Hays).
- **Stipend / Tuition**: Only a few fellowships list explicit amounts (NSF GRFP, Hertz, Spencer, Mellon/ACLS, DOE SCGSR). Many external fellowships do not provide stipend information in the source.

# Deadlines & Unknowns
- **Deadlines**: The source does not provide specific application windows or deadlines for most fellowships. The hoodie incentive refers to the 2025‑26 academic year but does not specify exact dates.
- **Application Windows**: For many external fellowships, the application period may vary by year and by awarding organization.
- **Eligibility Nuances**: Some fellowships encourage applications from historically underrepresented groups (e.g., Mellon/ACLS, Spencer). The exact criteria for underrepresentation are not detailed.
- **Funding Amounts**: Stipend and tuition amounts are only specified for a subset of fellowships. Others may have variable or unspecified support.

# Source Limitations
- The information is extracted from a single university webpage and may be incomplete or outdated.
- No explicit deadlines or application windows are listed for most fellowships.
- Stipend and tuition amounts are provided only where explicitly stated; other fellowships may have different or variable support.
- The hoodie incentive list is current for the 2025‑26 academic year but may change in future years.
- The article does not claim verification or guarantee of accuracy; it is a synthesis of publicly available data.

# Conclusion
Graduate students at UW‑Madison have access to a wide array of fellowships, both university‑funded and external. While some programs provide clear stipend and tuition support, many details—especially deadlines and nuanced eligibility—remain unspecified. Students are encouraged to consult the university’s Funding Forward program, the Grants & Funding micro‑course, the Grants Information Collection, and the Wisconsin Scholarship Hub for up‑to‑date application information. Contact your graduate program or the Associate Director of Graduate Funding for specific questions about eligibility and application procedures.

pages.description: Studying in the United States offers access to world-class education, but it also comes with high costs. Tuition, housing, insurance, and daily expenses can quickly add up for international students. This guide outlines how to find, shortlist, and apply for US scholarships.
pages.content:
# Scholarships for International Students in USA: A Comprehensive Guide

## Introduction
Studying in the United States offers access to world-class education but comes with high costs. Scholarships play a crucial role in alleviating financial pressure for international students. This guide outlines how to find, shortlist, and apply for US scholarships.

## What is a Scholarship?
Scholarships provide financial aid to students, typically not requiring repayment, to help manage costs like tuition, which can reach up to $80,000 annually for international students. Funding sources include universities, government bodies, and private institutions.

## Can International Students Study for Free?
While full-ride scholarships, merit-based aid, or tuition-free programs exist, they are highly competitive and rare. Even with a full tuition waiver, students usually need to cover living costs, insurance, and travel expenses.

## Who Can Apply?
Scholarships are available for:
*   Undergraduate students
*   Master's students
*   PhD and research scholars
*   MBA applicants
*   Medical and STEM students
*   Transfer students
*   Community college students

## Types of Scholarships Available
Scholarships vary based on academic records, financial need, and program of study.

### Merit-Based Scholarships
Awarded for exceptional academic records, leadership, athletic achievements, or extracurriculars. These can be full-ride, partial, or waivers.
*   **Fulbright Foreign Student Program**: Government-funded for students, artists, and young professionals globally.
*   **Aga Khan Foundation's International Scholarship Program**: For students with excellent academic records.

### Need-Based Scholarships
Awarded to students demonstrating financial need. Applicants often submit a CSS Profile.
*   **Harvard University Scholarships**: Offers up to 100% scholarship based on need and exceptional credentials.
*   **Amherst College Financial Aid**: Aid packages based on financial need.

### Fully Funded Scholarships
Cover the entire cost of studying and living in the US. Offered by government bodies, elite universities, and international foundations.
*   **Knight-Hennessy Scholars at Stanford University**: Covers tuition, living stipend, and enrichment for up to three years for graduate students globally.
*   **Karsh International Scholars Program at Duke University**: For international students demonstrating financial need and academic merit.

### Partial Scholarships
Cover a portion of the total cost, significantly reducing financial burden, especially when combined with other awards. More common than full-ride awards.
*   **Temple University Merit Scholarships**: $2,000 to $20,000 annually for high-achieving international undergraduate students for up to four years.
*   **Clark University Financial Aid**: Merit-based and need-based partial relief.

### Subject-Specific Scholarships
Awarded to students pursuing particular fields, often in high-demand disciplines. Competition may be less than for general scholarships.
*   **AAUW International Fellowship**: For women from outside the US pursuing full-time graduate or postdoctoral STEM study ($20,000-$25,000).
*   **University of Florida Humanities Fellowships and Grants**: Multiple options for international students in various programs.

### Diversity and Inclusion Scholarships
Support students from underrepresented backgrounds, regions, and communities to increase representation.
*   **Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program**: For academically talented African students with financial need and a commitment to community service, covering full costs at partner universities.
*   **Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program**: For mid-career professionals from World Bank member countries pursuing development-related graduate studies, covering full tuition, living allowance, and travel.

### Sports Scholarships
Offered through channels like the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) for students with exceptional athletic ability who compete at the collegiate level. Can cover partial to full tuition.
*   **NCAA Division I Athletic Scholarships**: Full or partial scholarships for various sports, covering tuition, room, board, and fees.
*   **NCAA Division II Athletic Scholarships**: Partial scholarships, offering a balance between athletics and academics.

### Research and Teaching Assistantships
Primarily for graduate students, these are funded positions where students contribute to research or teaching in exchange for tuition remission and a monthly stipend. Common in STEM, social sciences, and humanities.

## Who Offers Scholarships?
Scholarships are offered by:

### U.S. Government Scholarships
*   **Fulbright Foreign Student Program**:
    *   **Eligibility**: International students, young professionals, artists from over 160 countries.
    *   **Coverage**: Full tuition, living stipend, airfare, health insurance.
    *   **Degree level**: Master's and PhD (and non-degree postgraduate study).
    *   **Deadline**: Varies by country.
    *   **Competitiveness**: Highly competitive (over 4,000 awards annually).
    *   **Application**: Through home country's Fulbright Commission or US Embassy.
*   **Hubert H. Humphrey Fellowship Program**:
    *   **Eligibility**: Experienced mid-career professionals from designated developing countries.
    *   **Coverage**: Full funding for a 10-month non-degree academic program.
    *   **Focus**: Public policy, public health, education, journalism, law, and related fields.
    *   **Benefit**: Professional development and networking.
*   **Foreign Language Teaching Assistant (FLTA) Program**:
    *   **Eligibility**: Young teachers and advanced English students from abroad who teach their native language.
    *   **Coverage**: Stipend, housing support, academic coursework.
    *   **Commitment**: Teach native language part-time for one academic year.
    *   **Condition**: Strict no-dependent policy.

### Scholarships Offered by Universities
Many US universities, including Ivy League institutions and public state universities, provide scholarships, grants, and aid.
*   **Harvard Financial Aid**: Merit-based, need-blind admissions, meeting demonstrated financial need.
*   **Yale University Scholarships**: Need-blind admissions, fully meeting financial needs with no loans.
*   **Princeton University Grants**: All aid is grant-based, no loans.
*   **Duke University Karsh Scholarship**: Covers full tuition, room, board, and fees for students with financial need and academic excellence.
*   **Clark University Presidential Scholarship**: Covers full tuition, room, and board for four years (approximately five students annually).

### Private Organizations and Foundations
*   **Rotary Foundation Peace Fellowships**: Fully funded master's or professional development programs for peace and conflict resolution.
*   **AAUW International Fellowships**: For women from outside the US pursuing graduate or postdoctoral study at accredited US institutions.
*   **Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship**: For students from World Bank member countries pursuing development-related graduate studies.
*   **Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship**: For outstanding students from select developing countries pursuing postgraduate education abroad.

### Corporate and Industry Scholarships
*   **Google Scholarships**: Various programs, including Google Generation Scholarship for STEM students from underrepresented communities.
*   **Microsoft Scholarships**: For students in computer science and related fields, often tied to internship opportunities.
*   **Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program**: For African students pursuing undergraduate or graduate education at partner institutions.

### Country-Specific Scholarships
Scholarships for students from specific geographic areas.
*   **India**: Inlaks Shivdasani Foundation Scholarships, USIEF Fulbright-Nehru Fellowships, Tata Scholarship at Cornell.
*   **Africa**: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program, Aga Khan Foundation scholarships, African Graduate Fellowship.
*   **Southeast Asia**: East-West Center Graduate Degree Fellowship.
*   **Middle East**: AMIDEAST Education Abroad scholarships.

## Eligibility Criteria: What Universities Look For
Universities assess several factors for scholarship eligibility:

### Academic Requirements
*   **GPA**: Minimum 3.5 on a 4.0 scale for most merit scholarships; elite programs expect 3.8+.
*   **Standardized tests**: SAT or ACT for undergraduate; GRE or GMAT for graduate (many universities are now test-optional).
*   **Academic transcripts**: Official transcripts from all institutions attended, often requiring certified English translations and GPA conversion to the 4.0 US scale.

### English Language Requirements
*   **TOEFL iBT**: Typically 90-100+; elite institutions may require 100-110+.
*   **IELTS Academic**: 6.5-7.5 standard; top universities often expect 7.0+.
*   **Duolingo English Test**: 105-120+ generally accepted at universities that recognize it.
*   **Waivers**: Available to students whose prior degrees were taught entirely in English, or to native English speakers.

### Extracurricular Activities
*   Leadership roles in student organizations, clubs, or community groups.
*   Volunteering and community service, especially in under-resourced areas.
*   Demonstrated social impact or civic engagement.
*   Participation in national or international academic competitions.

### Work Experience
*   **MBA programs**: Typically require 3-5 years of professional experience.
*   **PhD applications**: Research experience, internships, and published work strengthen applications significantly.
*   **Industry experience**: Adds credibility to personal statements and career goals.

### Financial Documentation
*   **CSS Profile**: A detailed financial assessment required by most private universities.
*   **Bank statements**: Recent statements showing the family's financial standing.
*   **Proof of income**: Tax returns or income certificates from your home country.
*   **Sponsor letters**: If a family member, employer, or organization is funding part of your studies.

### Personal Qualities
*   Clear, authentic leadership profile with evidence of initiative and impact.
*   A compelling vision for social or professional impact in your community or field.
*   Research potential and intellectual curiosity, especially for graduate scholarships.
*   Strong written and verbal communication skills, reflected in essays and interviews.
*   Resilience and the ability to thrive in a new cultural and academic environment.

## Step-by-Step Process to Find Scholarships
1.  **Start Early**: Begin researching 18 months before your intended intake about universities and scholarship types.
2.  **Shortlist**: 12 months before intake, shortlist universities and scholarships; begin preparation for standardized test scores and language tests.
3.  **Draft Documents**: 6-9 months before intake, draft personal statements and collect recommendation letters and financial documents.
4.  **Cost Analysis**: Run a cost analysis including cost of attendance, living expenses, and tuition cost.
5.  **Apply**: Submit applications before deadlines and apply to multiple scholarships simultaneously. Do not stick to one option.
6.  **Track**: Track university scholarship applications and external scholarship applications separately.

## Documents Required for Scholarship Applications
*   **Academic Transcripts**: Transcripts from non-English-speaking countries typically require certified English translations. Some universities require a GPA conversion to the 4.0 US scale.
*   **Statement of Purpose (SOP) / Personal Statement**: Should open with a compelling hook, clearly state academic and professional background, explain career vision, include impact narrative, and be tailored to the specific scholarship and institution.
*   **Letters of Recommendation (LORs)**: For undergraduate, request from teachers. For graduate, at least one from a professor speaking to research ability. For MBA, a supervisor or manager speaking to leadership and professional impact.
*   **Resume / CV**: Clear formatting and chronology (education, experience, skills, awards). Quantify achievements. For PhD applicants, include publications, conference presentations, and research projects prominently.
*   **English Proficiency Scores**: Ensure TOEFL, IELTS, or Duolingo scores are valid and submitted directly from the testing body to target universities and scholarship programs. Check individual scholarship requirements.
*   **Financial Documents**: Fill CSS Profile carefully and accurately. Provide family income certificates or tax returns from your home country. Keep recent bank statements (ideally 3-6 months). Submit affidavit of support or sponsor letter if a family member is co-funding studies.
*   **Portfolio or Research Proposal (If Applicable)**: Arts program applicants should attach a portfolio of original work. Doctorate programs may require a well-developed research proposal identifying a clear research question, justifying its significance, and outlining methodology. STEM applicants should highlight prior research, patents, projects, or publications.

## What Reviewers Look for
*   Evidence of intellectual curiosity and the ability to think independently.
*   Demonstrated leadership and the ability to inspire or mobilize others.
*   A convincing and specific vision for how you will use your education to create impact.
*   Clarity of writing and the ability to communicate complex ideas persuasively.
*   Authenticity; avoid generic or AI-generated essays. Put good thought into writing a winning scholarship essay.

### Crafting a Powerful Personal Statement
*   **Hook**: Open with a specific moment, observation, or question that sparked your interest in your field.
*   **Background**: Briefly establish your academic and personal journey. Speak about what shaped you.
*   **Career Vision**: Where are you headed, and why does it matter to you and to the world?
*   **Why this scholarship and program**: Be specific. Mention the faculty, research centers, or program features that align with your goals.
*   **Closing**: Close your application with a forward-looking statement that reinforces your motivation and readiness.

## Common Application Mistakes
*   Writing a generic essay without considering the specific scholarship or program.
*   Relying completely on AI to generate essays.

pages.description: The National Science Foundation (NSF) offers a range of funding programs for graduate students, including fellowships, internships, and research grants. This article summarizes the main programs, eligibility criteria, funding amounts, application deadlines, and how to apply, based on the NSF’s official website.
pages.content:
Overview
The NSF provides financial support to graduate students and recent Ph.D.s through fellowships, internships, and research grants. These opportunities are designed to enhance research skills, broaden professional networks, and support training in STEM fields.

Key Programs
1. NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP)
   • Supports research‑based master’s or doctoral degrees in STEM or STEM education.
   • Five‑year fellowship with three years of financial support.
   • Includes an annual stipend and a cost‑of‑education allowance for tuition and fees.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents; full‑time research‑based enrollment at an accredited U.S. institution.
   • Application deadline: Fall of each year.

2. International Research Experiences for Students (IRES)
   • Provides international research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students.
   • Participants are mentored by researchers at foreign labs.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents.
   • Application: Contact researchers with IRES funding; materials vary by project.

3. Computer and Information Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowships (CSGrad4US)
   • Targets bachelor’s degree holders returning to academia for a research‑based doctoral program in CISE.
   • Three‑year fellowship with stipend and cost‑of‑education allowance.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents; not currently enrolled in a degree‑granting program and never enrolled in a doctoral program.
   • Application deadline: Typically spring or early summer.

4. Doctoral Dissertation Research Improvement Grants (DDRIG)
   • Grants for doctoral students to conduct significant data‑gathering or field research.
   • Award amounts typically range from $15,000 to $40,000 (excluding indirect costs).
   • Eligibility: Doctoral students at U.S. institutions; citizenship not required.
   • Application: Submitted through the student’s dissertation advisor; deadlines vary by program.

5. NSF Research Traineeship Program (NRT)
   • Provides at least 12‑month stipends for graduate students to develop skills for STEM careers.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents; enrolled in research‑based master’s or doctoral programs.
   • International students may participate as unfunded trainees.
   • Application: Contact researchers with NRT funding; use the NSF NRT Project Search.

6. Mathematical Sciences Graduate Internship
   • Summer research internships for doctoral students in mathematics, statistics, or applied mathematics.
   • Focus on applications outside academia, primarily at national laboratories.
   • Eligibility: Current doctoral students; citizenship not required.
   • Application deadline: Fall or winter each year.

7. Summer Scholars Internship Program
   • 10‑week summer internship for undergraduate and graduate students in NSF offices.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents.
   • Application: Through designated organizations such as QEM Network, Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities, or National Internship Program.

8. Postdoctoral Research Fellowships
   • Two‑ or three‑year fellowships for recent Ph.D.s to conduct independent research.
   • Eligibility: U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents who have earned or will earn a Ph.D. before the fellowship.
   • Application: Current opportunities listed on NSF’s Funding Search; deadlines vary.

How to Apply
- Identify the program that matches your research interests and eligibility.
- For fellowship programs, visit the specific program’s website (e.g., nsfgrfp.org for GRFP) for detailed application instructions.
- For internships and traineeships, locate active projects via the NSF Project Search tools (e.g., IRES Project Search, NRT Project Search).
- Contact the principal investigator or program coordinator for project‑specific application materials.

Eligibility Summary
- Most programs require U.S. citizenship, nationality, or permanent residency, except for DDRIG, IRES, and the Mathematical Sciences Graduate Internship, which do not require citizenship.
- Programs differ in required enrollment status (e.g., full‑time research‑based master’s or doctoral, or not currently enrolled for CSGrad4US).
- Some programs (e.g., DDRIG) require submission through a dissertation advisor.

Deadlines
- GRFP: Fall each year.
- CSGrad4US: Spring or early summer.
- DDRIG: Varies by program; some accept proposals year‑round.
- IRES, NRT, Mathematical Sciences Internship: Fall or winter.
- Summer Scholars Internship: Application period varies by partner organization.

Unknowns and Source Limitations
- The exact stipend amounts for each program are not specified in the source text.
- Specific application deadlines for many programs (e.g., DDRIG, NRT) are not listed; they vary by program.
- The source does not provide detailed eligibility nuances such as specific institutional requirements or funding limits.
- The information is based on a single snapshot of the NSF website; program details may change over time.

Conclusion
Graduate students seeking NSF funding should consult the individual program websites and NSF’s Funding Search for the most current and detailed information. While this article summarizes the main programs and eligibility criteria, applicants should verify all requirements and deadlines directly with NSF or the relevant program coordinator.

pages.description: A concise guide summarising the types, eligibility criteria, funding levels and known limitations of scholarships for international students as described in the Times Higher Education article (Mar 2026).
pages.content:
## Introduction
This article synthesises information from the Times Higher Education guide (published 9 Mar 2026, updated 18 Mar 2026) on scholarships for international students. The source is a broad‑scope guide and does not provide exhaustive, up‑to‑date listings of every award.

## What is a scholarship?
A scholarship is a financial award that can cover tuition, living costs, travel and academic materials. Awards may be based on academic merit, extracurricular achievement, research interests, leadership potential or financial need. They are available to undergraduate, postgraduate, research and PhD programmes.

## Where to find scholarships
1. **University‑offered scholarships** – set by each institution, often merit‑ or need‑based.
2. **Academic/merit‑based scholarships** – awarded for high grades or subject‑specific achievement.
3. **Performance‑based scholarships** – for excellence in sport, arts or music.
4. **External scholarships** – from businesses, charities or higher‑education associations, applied for separately from university admission.
5. **Government scholarships** – funded by national governments, sometimes targeted at specific source countries.
6. **Country/region‑based scholarships** – offered by a mix of universities, governments and organisations for students from particular nations or regions.

## Types of scholarships
- **Partially funded** – cover some expenses; students must source the remainder.
- **Fully funded** – cover tuition, accommodation and living costs for the full programme.
- **Research grants** – fund specific research projects.
- **Work‑study programmes** – combine employment with study funding.
- **Undergraduate vs postgraduate** – distinct awards exist for each level.

## How to apply (key steps)
1. Research all scholarship streams for the target country.
2. Verify eligibility (grades, nationality, financial need, field of study).
3. Maintain strong academic performance.
4. Participate in relevant extracurricular activities.
5. Gather required documents: acceptance letter, transcripts, proof of need, English test scores, recommendation letters.
6. Write a personal statement tailored to the scholarship.
7. Proofread and submit well before the deadline.
8. Track multiple applications and deadlines in a spreadsheet.

## Regional scholarship examples (as listed in the source)
- **United Kingdom**
  - *UCL and Imperial College London* – scholarships for Indian students (specific criteria not detailed).
  - *UK Government AI scholarship & visa package* – for international undergraduates, doctoral candidates and early‑career researchers in AI/data science.
  - *Rhodes Scholarship* – postgraduate study at Oxford for any nationality.
  - *Chevening* – fully funded master’s scholarships for students from ~160 countries.
  - *University of Birmingham Commonwealth Scholarship* – £3,000 award for Commonwealth nationals enrolled in a master’s programme (deducted from tuition).
  - *GREAT Scholarships* – funding for students from 15 countries (details not specified).
- **United States**
  - *MPOWER Financing Global Citizens Fund* – up to US$10,000 for refugees, DACA and international students.
  - *Fulbright Foreign Student Program* – long‑standing government scholarship for graduate study.
  - *Scholarships at HBCUs* – e.g., Thurgood Marshall College Fund, UNCF, Congressional Black Caucus Foundation, National Racial Equity Initiative (eligibility varies).
- **Australia & New Zealand**
  - *Pinnacle Foundation* – scholarships and mentorship for LGBTQIA+ students in Australia.
  - *Monash International Leadership Scholarship* – tuition‑fee coverage for successful applicants.
  - *Australia Awards Scholarships* – fully funded for students from Africa and the Indo‑Pacific (undergraduate and postgraduate).
  - *Manaaki New Zealand Scholarships* – funding for study at New Zealand universities.
- **Canada**
  - *MPOWER Financing Global Citizens Fund* – up to C$10,000 for refugees, DACA and international students.
  - *John M. Kerr Memorial Bursary* – supports 2SLGBTQIA+ students in Alberta.
- **Europe (selected countries)**
  - *HEC Imagine Fellows* – master’s students from war‑torn countries for study at HEC Paris.
  - *DAAD Master’s Scholarship* – German government funding for international students.
  - *Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters* – multi‑university funding across Europe.  - *NL Scholarship* – for non‑EEA students pursuing bachelor’s or master’s in the Netherlands.
- **Global programmes**
  - *Mastercard Foundation Scholarship Programme* – funding and mentorship for African students.
  - *World Bank Scholarship Programme* – for development‑related master’s studies.
  - *Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship* – limited awards for select countries.
  - *Google Generation Scholarships* – for computer‑science, gaming and technology studies.
  - *IELTS Prize* – £3,000 towards tuition for IELTS test‑takers.

## Known eligibility criteria (from the source)
- Academic merit (high grades, GPA, subject‑specific scores).
- Country or region of residence (e.g., Commonwealth, specific partner countries for GREAT, DAAD, etc.).
- Field of study (STEM, arts, leadership, AI, etc.).
- Financial need (where required).
- Specific demographic groups (refugees, DACA, LGBTQIA+, students with disabilities, war‑torn‑country nationals).
- Level of study (undergraduate, master’s, PhD, research).

## Funding details (as reported)
- Fully funded scholarships may cover tuition, accommodation, living expenses and travel.
- Partially funded awards may cover tuition only or a portion of living costs.
- Specific monetary amounts mentioned: £3,000 (Birmingham Commonwealth), up to US$10,000 (MPOWER US), up to C$10,000 (MPOWER Canada), £3,000 (IELTS Prize), £1,000‑£2,500 for various UK engineering scholarships.

## Deadlines
The source does **not** provide concrete application deadlines for the listed programmes. Applicants must consult the individual scholarship webpages for up‑to‑date deadline information.

## Unknowns and source limitations
- The guide was last updated March 2026; scholarship terms, amounts and eligibility may have changed since then.
- No comprehensive list of all scholarships is provided; many national or institutional awards are omitted.
- Specific application procedures, required documents and exact deadline dates are not detailed.
- Funding amounts are only given for a few examples; most scholarships lack disclosed monetary values.
- The article includes advertising placeholders (e.g., “ADVERTISEMENT”) that may interrupt the flow of information.

## Frequently Asked Questions (selected)
1. **How do scholarships work?** – Awards are granted based on criteria such as merit, need, nationality or research focus and may cover part or all of study costs.
2. **How to apply?** – Identify suitable scholarships, meet eligibility, prepare documents (transcripts, statements, references) and submit before the deadline.
3. **Where to find them?** – University websites, government portals, scholarship databases, and guides like THE Student.
4. **What do they cover?** – Tuition, accommodation, books, travel, and living costs, depending on the award.
5. **Do they cover all expenses?** – Some are fully funded; many are partial. Review each award’s terms.

*This article presents only the information explicitly available in the source text and does not guarantee completeness or current accuracy.*

pages.content:
Overview
The Frederick S. Pardee School of Global Studies at Boston University offers master’s programs for students worldwide. This guide extracts confirmed facts from the school’s official admissions page (https://www.bu.edu/pardeeschool/admissions/graduate-admissions/application-instructions/) as of 2026‑11‑12 and highlights what remains unknown.

Confirmed Eligibility
- A four‑year bachelor’s degree from a recognized institution, or an equivalent international qualification, satisfies the basic academic requirement. [Confirmed]
- A three‑year bachelor’s degree from an Indian institution accredited by NAAC is also accepted. [Confirmed]

Application Materials [Confirmed]
- Completed online application (US$95 fee).
- Unofficial transcripts from all prior universities.
- Three letters of recommendation.
- Statement of purpose (~500 words).
- Résumé or curriculum vitae.
- English‑proficiency evidence if exemption criteria are not met (see below).

English‑Proficiency Requirements [Confirmed]
Exempt if any of the following apply:
  * Native English speaker.
  * Bachelor’s studies conducted entirely in English.
  * Four+ years of full‑time work in an English‑speaking environment.
Otherwise, submit one of the following tests:
  * TOEFL iBT: minimum 90 total (22 per section) – new reports (from Jan 2026) require 5 overall with ≥4.5 each component.
  * IELTS Academic: overall 7.0, minimum 6.5 each band.
  * Cambridge C1‑level exams (B2 First Grade A, C1 Advanced A/B, C2 Proficiency passing).
  * Duolingo: minimum 130 (must select BU Graduate & Professional Programs as recipient and email admissions). [Confirmed]

Application Deadlines [Confirmed]
Spring 2027:
  • Sep 1 2026 – application portal opens.
  • Nov 15 2026 – priority‑aid deadline.
  • Dec 1 2026 – final deadline for international applicants (all documents required).
  • Dec 15 2026 – final deadline for domestic applicants.
Fall 2027:
  • Sep 1 2026 – portal opens.
  • Jan 15 2027 – first priority‑aid deadline.
  • Mar 15 2027 – second priority‑aid deadline.
  • Jul 15 2027 – final deadline for international applicants.
  • Jul 30 2027 – final deadline for domestic applicants.
All dates are listed in the source and are therefore confirmed.

Dual‑Degree Programs [Confirmed]
- IR/JD (with BU Law) and IR/MBA (with Questrom) require separate applications to each school. Admission is contingent on acceptance by both. Program‑specific requirements must be verified with the respective schools.

Timeline for International Students [Confirmed]
- Apply at least three months before program start to allow visa processing.
- Student visas may be issued up to 120 days before start date, but entry is permitted only 30 days prior.

Funding & Aid [Partial Confirmation]
- The page mentions “priority aid consideration” deadlines but provides no details on scholarship amounts, eligibility criteria, or guaranteed funding. Therefore, specific financial‑aid information is unknown.

Unknowns & Source Limitations
- Exact tuition costs, scholarship amounts, and eligibility criteria are not disclosed on the referenced page.
- Availability of program‑specific scholarships or assistantships is not addressed.
- Any changes after the page’s last update (post‑Nov 2026) are not captured.
- The source does not list GRE/GMAT requirements for non‑dual‑degree programs beyond noting GRE is not required.

Practical Checklist for International Applicants
- [ ] Verify bachelor’s degree meets the four‑year or NAAC‑accredited three‑year criteria.
- [ ] Register on the BU graduate application portal (opens Sep 1 2026).
- [ ] Pay the $95 application fee.
- [ ] Upload unofficial transcripts for all prior institutions.
- [ ] Request three recommendation letters and ensure they are uploaded before the deadline.
- [ ] Draft a 500‑word statement of purpose tailored to the Pardee School.
- [ ] Prepare a résumé/CV.
- [ ] Assess English‑proficiency exemption; if not exempt, schedule and complete TOEFL/IELTS/Cambridge/Duolingo and send scores to BU (use institution code 3087 for TOEFL).
- [ ] For dual‑degree interest, review LSAT/GRE/GMAT requirements with the partner school.
- [ ] Submit all materials by Dec 1 2026 (international) or Dec 15 2026 (domestic) for Spring 2027, or by Jul 15/30 2027 for Fall 2027.
- [ ] Contact psgsadm@bu.edu with any questions or for assistance.

How to Verify Current Information
- Visit the official admissions page at https://www.bu.edu/pardeeschool/admissions/graduate-admissions/application-instructions/.

pages.content:
# What Are Graduate Grants?
Graduate grants are non‑repayable funds awarded to students pursuing advanced degrees. They are typically awarded based on financial need, academic performance, research goals, or a combination of these factors.

# Eligibility
- Enrollment in an accredited college or university.
- Some awards require a minimum GPA, specific degree program, or research focus.
- Certain grants target specific demographics (e.g., underrepresented racial groups, women) or fields of study.

# Types of Grants
## Federal Grants
- **Teacher Education Assistance for College and Higher Education (TEACH) Grant** – Up to $4,000; deadline: late October; requires a 3.25 GPA or 75th percentile exam score and a commitment to teach in low‑income schools for at least four years.
- **Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant** – Up to $6,095; deadline varies; available to students whose parent or guardian died during military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after 9/11, 2001.
- **Fulbright Grants** – Award amounts and deadlines vary; designed for international study and research.

## State Grants
- **Colorado Graduate Grant** – Up to $5,000 for students demonstrating financial need.
- **Ohio Department of Natural Resources Grant** – $2,000 for earth science graduate students conducting research.

## School‑Specific Grants
- **California State University System State University Grant Program** – Available to CSU students.
- **Michigan State University University Fellowship Programs** – Funding for master’s and doctoral fine arts students.

## Professional and Corporate Grants
- **American Cancer Society Doctoral Training Grants in Oncology Social Work** – $20,000 for two‑year doctoral social work students researching oncology.
- **Geological Society of America Graduate Student Research Grants** – Up to $5,000 for geological sciences students; membership required.
- **University Film and Video Association Carole Fielding Student Grant** – Up to $1,000 for film and televisual arts students; requires faculty sponsorship.

## Minority and Women Grants
- **American Anthropological Association AAA Minority Dissertation Fellowship** – $10,000 for doctoral anthropology students from underrepresented racial groups.
- **American Society of Criminology Ruth D. Peterson Fellowship** – $6,000 for minority doctoral students in criminal justice or criminology.
- **Wisconsin Higher Educational Aids Board Indian Student Assistance Grant** – Up to $1,100 for graduate students who are at least 25 % Native American.
- **American Association of University Women Career Development Grants** – Up to $12,000 for women in advanced degree programs; deadline: mid‑November.
- **American Physical Society M. Hildred Blewett Fellowship** – Up to $45,000 for female physics doctoral students returning after a hiatus; deadline: early June.
- **Zonta International Foundation Amelia Earhart Fellowship** – $10,000 for women in aerospace doctoral programs; deadline varies.

## Field‑Specific Grants
- **American Psychological Association Grants in Aid for Students** – Up to $1,000 for psycholegal research; deadline: late September.
- **National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program** – $34,000 for research‑based STEM graduate students; deadline: late October.
- **Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education Program Graduate Student Grant** – Up to $15,000 for master’s and doctoral students researching sustainable agriculture; project duration up to 36 months.

# Tips for Applicants
1. **Search Profession‑Specific Organizations** – Many professional associations offer grants to support their workforce.
2. **Polish Your Writing** – Use consistent fonts, proper grammar, and avoid abbreviations.
3. **Explain a Low GPA** – If GPA is below the minimum, provide a narrative explaining other strengths.
4. **Tailor Each Application** – Customize responses rather than copy‑pasting.
5. **Build Faculty Relationships** – Early contact with program faculty can clarify funding availability.
6. **Continue Searching** – Grants are offered year‑round; persistent searching can reduce tuition costs.

# Additional Resources
- Understanding Financial Aid for Graduate School
- Top Scholarships for Graduate Students
- Paying for Your Master’s Degree
- Paying for Your PhD

# Source Limitations and Unknowns
- The information originates from a single website; no external verification of award amounts, eligibility, or deadlines.
- Several deadlines are listed as “varies” or not specified, indicating that applicants should consult the issuing organization directly.
- Award amounts for some grants (e.g., Fulbright, certain professional grants) are not disclosed.
- The data may be outdated; the website’s last update is not indicated.

# Read Time
Approximately 8 minutes (based on 1,200 words and average reading speed of 200 words per minute).

pages.content:
Eligibility
International students are generally not eligible for federal or state financial aid programs, which require U.S. citizenship, U.S. national status, or permanent residency. They may receive institutional aid, scholarships, fellowships, and assistantships offered by the university. Private loans are available only if a U.S. citizen or permanent resident can serve as a co‑signer.

Undergraduate Students
Undergraduates may be considered for scholarships awarded by colleges or departments. These scholarships are typically awarded automatically based on the admission file and academic records; no separate application is required.

Graduate Students
Graduate admission automatically places applicants in consideration for all university‑administered fellowships and assistantships. Many departments award financial aid concurrently with admission, so it is advisable to submit all required materials by the admission deadline. Academic excellence is the primary criterion; financial need is rarely a factor.

Fellowships
Most campus fellowships are awarded to students beginning graduate studies in the fall. The Graduate College maintains a searchable list of fellowship opportunities from the university and external sources. Fellowships are only available to full‑time, degree‑seeking students and are contingent on available funding. Awardees receive tuition waivers and selected fee waivers.

Assistantships
Teaching, research, graduate, and pre‑professional assistants receive stipends for services rendered to the university. To hold an assistantship, students must be registered for the semester of appointment and maintain good academic standing. Teaching assistantships require proficiency in oral English as defined by university verification standards.

Scholarship Opportunities
Students can search for external scholarships through online search engines and resources such as International Education Financial Aid, International Scholarships Online, and The SmartStudent Guide to Studying in the USA.

Student Loans
Limited private alternative loans are available, but most lenders require a U.S. citizen or permanent resident co‑signer. A comprehensive list of international private loan lenders is provided by the university.

Employment Opportunities
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) strictly regulates employment for international students. For guidance, contact International Student and Scholar Services (ISSS).

Other Aid
The Office of Student Financial Aid offers additional resources, including grants, waivers, and employment assistance. Contact information: Arcade 620 East John Street, Champaign, IL 61820; 217‑333‑0100; finaid@illinois.edu.

Known Eligibility
• Not eligible for federal or state aid.
• Eligible for institutional scholarships, fellowships, and assistantships.
• Private loans require a U.S. citizen or permanent resident co‑signer.

Funding Options
• Institutional scholarships (undergraduate and graduate).
• Campus fellowships (full‑time graduate students).
• Teaching, research, and graduate assistantships.
• Limited private loans.

Deadlines
• Fellowships and assistantships are awarded concurrently with admission; submit all materials by the admission deadline.
• Specific fellowship and assistantship deadlines vary by department and are not listed in the source.

Unknowns
• Exact amounts of tuition waivers and stipend levels.
• Detailed application procedures for each scholarship or fellowship.
• Current availability of private loan options.

Source Limitations
The information is drawn from a single university webpage and may be outdated. No external verification or links are provided. The article does not claim to be exhaustive or definitive.

pages.title: Who Is Considered a Student? Global Perspectives on Eligibility, Funding, and Enrollment
pages.focus_keyword: Who Is Considered a Student? Global Perspectives on Eligibility, Funding, and Enrollment
pages.description: A concise overview of how the term “student” is defined worldwide, the typical eligibility requirements, common funding models, and the variability of enrollment deadlines, based on publicly available information.
pages.content:
Introduction
The word “student” appears in many contexts, from primary school pupils to university scholars. While the basic idea—someone enrolled in an educational institution—remains constant, eligibility, funding, and enrollment timelines differ markedly across countries and education levels.

Defining a Student
In most English‑speaking regions, a student is anyone enrolled in a recognized school, college, or university. The Wikipedia excerpt notes that in the United Kingdom and many Commonwealth nations the term applies mainly to secondary and higher education, whereas younger learners are called “pupils.” In non‑English contexts, distinct terms exist (e.g., Finnish "opiskelija" for university students, "oppilas" for compulsory‑education learners).

Eligibility Criteria Across Regions
* General rule: enrollment in a government‑approved or accredited institution.
* Age limits: primary education is typically compulsory for children aged 5‑12 (e.g., Singapore, Bangladesh), while secondary education often extends to ages 16‑18.
* Residency or citizenship requirements vary; some systems (e.g., Nigeria’s 6‑3‑3‑4 structure) accept any resident, while others may restrict university admission to citizens or permanent residents.
* Special categories: polytechnics, colleges of education, and vocational schools have separate eligibility pathways in several countries (e.g., Nigeria, South Africa).

Funding Mechanisms
* Public funding: many nations provide free or heavily subsidised primary and secondary education (e.g., Bangladesh, Brunei, Cambodia). The excerpt mentions free education in Brunei and Cambodia.
* Higher education: funding is more heterogeneous. Some countries offer tuition‑free university study (e.g., Finland for EU residents), while others rely on tuition fees and scholarships.
* Scholarships and grants: eligibility often depends on academic merit, financial need, or specific demographic criteria, but the source text does not list concrete programs.

Enrollment Deadlines and Academic Calendars
* Academic years differ: the United Kingdom typically starts in September, whereas Australia’s school year begins in late January or early February.
* Enrollment periods are set by individual institutions and may align with national school calendars. The Wikipedia excerpt does not provide specific deadline dates, indicating that these details must be obtained from local education authorities.

Unknowns and Data Gaps
* The source material contains numerous country‑specific descriptions but lacks uniform data on enrollment deadlines, scholarship amounts, or precise eligibility thresholds.
* Several sections of the excerpt are flagged as unsourced, suggesting that some statements may not be fully reliable.
* Information on private versus public funding ratios, especially for tertiary education, is missing.

Source Limitations
* The article is derived from a Wikipedia page that aggregates information from many contributors; some passages are marked with "[citation needed]" and may not be verifiable.
* The excerpt focuses on structural descriptions rather than quantitative data (e.g., funding amounts, enrollment statistics).
* Language variations and local terminology are summarized but not exhaustively covered.

Conclusion
The concept of a student is globally recognised but locally nuanced. Eligibility generally hinges on enrollment in an accredited institution, while funding ranges from fully public provision at the primary level to mixed public‑private models in higher education. Enrollment deadlines are institution‑specific and reflect national academic calendars. Researchers and policymakers should treat the available information as a starting point and seek up‑to‑date, locally sourced data for precise program design.

## Introduction
The personal statement is a central component of most U.S. college applications, typically limited to 650 words and submitted through the Common Application, Coalition Application, or school‑specific portals. The source material from College Essay Guy (updated 10/12/2026) offers a step‑by‑step framework for brainstorming, drafting, and revising this essay.

## Who Is Eligible?
- Applicants to colleges that accept the Common Application or similar platforms.
- Students seeking scholarship consideration where a personal statement is required (the source notes that scholarship committees may also use the essay).
- No specific age, citizenship, or GPA requirements are mentioned; eligibility is tied to the college application process itself.

## Funding and Costs

- No public funding or scholarship information is provided for accessing the guide itself; it appears freely available on the website.

## Typical Deadlines
- The article does not list exact application deadlines. Deadlines vary by institution and are usually in November (early decision) or January (regular decision) for most U.S. colleges.
- Readers should consult individual college admission calendars for precise dates.

## Core Advice from the Source
### What Is a Personal Statement?
- An essay that showcases a student’s qualities, skills, values, and motivations.
- Distinct from supplemental essays; it serves as the “heart” of the application.

### Qualities of Strong Essays
1. **Core Values** – Demonstrates 4‑5 distinct values (e.g., humor, community, autonomy).
2. **Vulnerability** – Shows personal honesty and emotional depth.
3. **Insight & Growth** – Includes “so what” moments that reflect learning.
4. **Craft** – Polished language, logical flow, and multiple drafts (minimum five recommended).

### Brainstorming Techniques
- Values Exercise, Essence Objects Exercise, 21 Details Exercise, and others.
- Two structural approaches: **Narrative** (challenge‑focused) and **Montage** (thematic collection of experiences).

### Writing Process
1. **Outline** – Essential before drafting; narrative outlines challenges, actions, lessons; montage outlines thematic threads.
2. **First Draft** – Write without worrying about word count; treat it as a brain dump.
3. **Revision** – At least five drafts, read aloud, seek external feedback, focus on transitions and opening/closing.

## Conclusion
The College Essay Guy article offers a comprehensive, experience‑based roadmap for crafting a personal statement, covering brainstorming, structure, drafting, and revision. While the guidance is practical, readers should verify any claims with additional sources, consider individual college requirements, and be aware of the lack of quantitative evidence supporting the suggested methods.

pages.content:
# TheDream.US National Scholarship for Immigrant Students

## Introduction
TheDream.US provides a National Scholarship designed to support first‑generation immigrant students—often referred to as Dreamers—who are undocumented or hold DACA/TPS status. The scholarship is described as a “Pell Grant” equivalent for students who qualify for in‑state tuition in their home state (excluding private, online, or Texas institutions). The program claims to cover tuition and fees up to $33,000 for a bachelor’s degree and offers an additional stipend of up to $6,000 for books, supplies, and transportation.

## Eligibility Criteria
The scholarship lists several eligibility requirements. These are the conditions that applicants must meet, according to the source text:

1. **Immigration Status** – First‑generation immigrant student who is currently undocumented, with or without DACA or TPS, who entered the United States before November 1, 2020, and before the age of 16.
2. **Continuous Residence** – Must have continuously lived in the United States since arrival.
3. **Financial Need** – Must have significant unmet financial need. Applicants who are receiving or eligible for the Federal Pell Grant are ineligible.
4. **High‑School Completion** – Must have graduated or will graduate from a U.S. high school (or earn a high‑school equivalency diploma) before the fall of 2026.
5. **Academic Performance** – High‑school GPA of 2.5 or better on a 4.0 scale; if college credits have been earned, a cumulative college GPA of 2.5 or better.
6. **Enrollment Intent** – Intend to enroll full‑time in an associate or bachelor’s program at a partner college in the student’s state in the fall of 2026 or spring of 2027.
7. **In‑State Tuition Eligibility** – Must be eligible for in‑state tuition at the partner college. The scholarship does not apply to private partner colleges in the state, online partner colleges, or if the student lives in Texas (see partner college list).

## Funding Details
The scholarship provides:

- **Tuition and Fees** – Up to **$33,000** for a bachelor’s degree at a partner college.
- **Stipend** – Up to **$6,000** for books, supplies, and transportation.
- **Renewal** – The award follows students through the completion of a bachelor’s degree and is renewable each year, contingent on meeting continuing eligibility criteria and renewing in June.

## Application Process
The application timeline and steps are outlined as follows:

- **Application Window** – Opens **November 1, 2025** and closes **February 28, 2026**.
- **Notification** – Award notifications are expected in **late April 2026**.
- **Acceptance** – Scholars must accept the award by the specified deadline.
- **Guide** – A step‑by‑step Application Guide is available for download.

Applicants are encouraged to use the guide to determine eligibility, complete the application, submit it, monitor status, and accept the award.

## Contact Information
- **Email** – [email protected] (reference “TheDream.US National Scholarship Program” in the subject line)
- **Phone** – 1‑855‑376‑7076 (ask for the TheDream.US National Scholarship Program)

## Known Uncertainties and Source Limitations
- **Date Conflicts** – The source text states that the scholarship is currently closed and that the next round opens on November 1, 2026, yet later it lists an opening date of November 1, 2025. The correct timeline is unclear.
- **Partner College List** – The specific partner colleges and the criteria for in‑state tuition eligibility are not provided in the excerpt.
- **Renewal Criteria** – While renewal is mentioned, the exact continuing eligibility requirements are not detailed.
- **Verification** – The information is taken directly from the source text and has not been independently verified. Users should consult the official TheDream.US website or contact the program directly for confirmation.

## Conclusion
TheDream.US’s National Scholarship offers significant financial support to first‑generation immigrant students who meet strict eligibility criteria. Applicants should carefully review the requirements, verify dates, and consult the official program resources before applying.

pages.content:
# Overview
The University of Memphis Graduate School offers several avenues for graduate students to finance their education. These include tuition and fee waivers, merit‑based scholarships, graduate assistantships, and external grant opportunities. The following sections summarize the primary funding options, eligibility requirements, and known deadlines.

# Tuition & Fees
- Full‑time graduate study requires a minimum of 9 credit hours (unless a late‑stage doctoral student). 
- The Graduate School provides a cost‑of‑attendance calculator at https://umwa.memphis.edu/estimator/. 
- The Council of Graduate Schools offers a financial‑planning resource, including a debt‑to‑earnings calculator, at https://gradsense.org.

# Non‑Resident Merit Scholarship
- Award: $2,100 per semester (fall & spring) for a total of $4,200 per academic year.
- Eligibility:
  * Non‑resident of Tennessee (U.S. citizen, permanent resident, or F‑1/J‑1 visa holder).
  * Charged the non‑resident or international tuition rate.
  * Admitted to a graduate degree program (excluding law school and graduate certificates).
  * Minimum cumulative undergraduate GPA of 3.25 (U.S.A. equivalent) or a completed master’s GPA; OR GRE score of 310 with at least 150 in Verbal and Quantitative and 2.5 AWA (or equivalent GMAT).
  * Must maintain full‑time enrollment each fall and spring; if below full‑time in the last semester, the award is prorated.
  * Must earn a 3.0 GPA at the University of Memphis each semester.
- The scholarship is admissions‑based; no separate application is required beyond the admission application.
- Students receiving graduate assistantships or other university funding (including non‑resident tuition waivers) are ineligible.

# Part‑Time Master’s Graduate Scholarship
- Award: $4,000 total ($2,000 each semester) toward tuition and fees.
- Up to 10 awards per academic year.
- Eligibility:
  * Minimum undergraduate GPA of 3.25.
  * Admitted to or currently enrolled in a Master’s program.
  * Strong letters of recommendation.
- Nomination Process: Departments recommend candidates to the Dean of their college or school; the Dean forwards ranked candidates to the Dean of the Graduate School.
- Terms:
  * Must maintain a cumulative GPA of 3.0 to receive second‑term funding.
  * Limited to one year.
  * Cannot hold a graduate assistantship or be employed by the university.
  * Must enroll for a minimum of 3 credit hours and a maximum of 8.
- Deadline: Rolling; awards are made for fall and spring semesters as funds allow.

# Border County Tuition Waivers
- Waiver of the non‑resident portion of tuition for students from specific border counties.
- Eligible counties:
  * Arkansas: Crittenden County.
  * Mississippi: DeSoto, Marshall, Tunica, Tate counties.
- Eligibility:
  * Admitted to a degree‑seeking program or non‑degree option.
  * Must provide documented proof of permanent residence in an eligible county.
- Application: Send proof to graduateadmissions@memphis.edu.

# Graduate Assistantships
## Full‑Time Graduate Assistantships
- Work average: 20 hours/week (half‑time employee).
- Includes full tuition, fees, health insurance (starting fall 2024), and a stipend.
- Requires full‑time enrollment (9 credit hours) unless at late‑stage doctoral, last semester of master’s, or thesis hours.
- Health insurance available after 4 months of contract.

## Part‑Time Graduate Assistantships
- Work average: 10 hours/week.
- Tuition levels and stipends vary; health insurance not available.
- Requires enrollment of at least 3 credit hours (or 1 credit hour for dissertation/thesis stage).
- Summer enrollment not required unless a new student.

- Assistantships are highly competitive and offered primarily through graduate programs or departments.
- Students should contact their department to verify availability and eligibility.

# Non‑Resident Waiver
- Out‑of‑state students may receive in‑state tuition rates for part‑time enrollment (≤8 credit hours) if employed full‑time (≥37.5 hours/week) in Tennessee.
- Requires a letter of employment on company letterhead each semester, submitted to graduateadmissions@memphis.edu by the final registration deadline.
- Students may take up to 8 credit hours; exceeding this forfeits the waiver.
