pages.title: Fordham GSAS International Student Admissions Guide
pages.focus_keyword: Fordham GSAS International Student Admissions Guide
pages.description: Fordham University's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) welcomes international applicants. This guide outlines key requirements for admission, including academic qualifications, English proficiency, credential evaluations, and the visa application process. It also highlights important deadlines and contact information.
pages.content:
## Introduction

Fordham University's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) accepts applications from international students globally. Applicants residing outside the U.S. are strongly encouraged to submit complete applications by their program's earliest deadline to allow sufficient time for the visa process.

## Applicant Requirements

To be considered for admission, applicants must hold an undergraduate degree (U.S. baccalaureate or equivalent) from an accredited institution prior to enrollment. International applicants with a three-year bachelor's degree from a Bologna Process member institution are eligible to apply to GSAS programs.

### Academic Transcripts and Credential Evaluations

Transcripts from previously attended post-secondary institutions must be submitted in English or accompanied by a certified English translation. For institutions outside the United States, Canada, Australia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, a course-by-course credential evaluation is strongly encouraged.

A course-by-course credential evaluation is required for applicants to the PhD programs in Psychology. If an institution is not part of the Bologna Process, an official course-by-course evaluation of higher education history from an international credential evaluation company that is a member of NACES (National Association of Credential Evaluation Services) or AICE (Association of International Credential Evaluators) is necessary. Evaluations typically take 2-4 weeks.

Waivers for credential evaluations may be considered on a case-by-case basis for programs where they are not required, provided the transcript meets specific criteria: it must be from a four-year program, written in English, include a comprehensive list of courses and credits with grades, and contain an explanatory key for the grading and credit system. The decision for a waiver rests with the Office of Admissions. The credential evaluation requirement for PhD programs in Psychology cannot be waived.

## English Proficiency Requirements

International applicants whose native language is not English must submit official test scores from one of the following accepted English language competency exams: TOEFL (iBT, Home Edition, Essentials, or Paper Edition if less than two years old), IELTS, Duolingo English Test (DET), PTE Academic, or Cambridge English Qualifications (B2 First, C1 Advanced, or C2 Proficiency exams).

Minimum score requirements vary by program:

*   **General GSAS Programs:** TOEFL iBT 100 (before January 21, 2026) or 5.0 (on or after January 21, 2026), IELTS 7.0, DET 130, PTE Academic 68, Cambridge English Qualifications 185.
*   **Specific Programs (PhD Computer Science, MS Computer Science, MS Cybersecurity, MS Data Science, Advanced Certificate in Data Science for Cybersecurity):** TOEFL iBT 85 (before January 21, 2026) or 4.5 (on or after January 21, 2026), IELTS 6.5, DET 115, PTE Academic 59, Cambridge English Qualifications 176.

Official scores should be sent directly by the testing service to the Office of Graduate Admissions (Fordham's ETS TOEFL score is #2259).

### Exemptions to the English Language Requirement

Exemptions are considered on a case-by-case basis for applicants who are native English speakers from countries where English is an official language, or who have completed, within the past five years, at least two years of study at an undergraduate or graduate institution in the United States or a country where English is the official language of instruction. An exemption may also be considered for applicants who received an undergraduate or graduate degree from a university in India, though language proficiency test scores may still be requested in some cases. GSAS reserves the right to require a language proficiency evaluation from any applicant.

### Fordham English Language Test (FELT) Condition

Students whose English proficiency scores do not meet GSAS program requirements may be required to take the Fordham English Language Test (FELT), administered by Fordham's Institute of American Language and Culture (IALC). Additional coursework may also be recommended by the IALC. Students admitted with this condition are permitted to register for two GSAS courses during the academic term in which they are completing IALC-recommended coursework.

## Funding and Costs

Tuition costs associated with the learning of English as a second language are the responsibility of the student and are not covered by GSAS tuition scholarships. GSAS merit-based tuition scholarships are not applicable to the costs of additional coursework recommended by the IALC.

## Immigration and Visas

International students must obtain a Form I-20 or Form DS-2019 from the Fordham Office of International Services to apply for an F-1 Student Visa or a J-1 Exchange Visa. GSAS Admissions does not issue these forms.

Upon accepting an offer of admission, international applicants will be instructed to upload a completed and signed Affidavit of Support (AFCOE), accompanied by original supporting documentation (e.g., passport identification, bank statements, scholarship award letters), directly to their application. Financial documentation must verify adequate resources to cover tuition, fees, and living expenses for the full-time program. Any document not in English must have a certified translation. Admissions will transfer these documents to the Office of International Services for I-20 or DS-2019 processing.

### Deadlines for Visa Processing

To avoid visa delays, it is vital to submit the completed AFCOE and supporting documents as soon as possible after accepting an offer of admission. Recommended submission dates are:

*   **Spring Admission:** No later than December 1
*   **Fall Admission:** No later than July 1

## Important Contact Information

*   **Visas and Immigration:** `[email protected]`
*   **Course Registration, Payroll Forms, Social Security Numbers for GSAS Merit-Based Financial Aid:** `[email protected]`
*   **Application and Admissions Process:** `[email protected]`

While it recommends applying by the earliest program deadline, specific program application deadlines are not detailed within this text. Exact costs of attendance are not specified, though applicants are required to demonstrate financial capacity to cover them. The source mentions external websites for visa information but does not provide direct links or guarantee the accuracy of information found on those external sites.

pages.title: Federal Student Aid for International Study
pages.focus_keyword: Federal Student Aid for International Study
pages.description: Federal student aid can be used for study‑abroad programs or full degree programs outside the United States, but eligibility depends on meeting FAFSA criteria, attending a U.S. school that participates in federal aid, and the student’s level (undergraduate, graduate, professional). Funding limits, application steps, and repayment rules are outlined by the Department of Education, though many details vary by school and program.
pages.content:
## Overview
The U.S. Department of Education allows eligible students to use federal student aid for two main types of international education:
1. Short‑term study‑abroad programs (semester or year).
2. Full degree programs at foreign institutions that participate in the Direct Loan Program.

## Eligibility
- Must be eligible for federal student aid under the standard FAFSA criteria.
- Must be enrolled at a U.S. school that participates in federal student aid; if the U.S. school does not participate, aid cannot be used abroad.
- Student status matters: undergraduate, graduate, and professional students have different loan limits and eligibility rules.
- For study‑abroad programs, the program must be approved by the U.S. school’s financial‑aid office.
- For full‑degree programs, the foreign school must be listed as a participating school in the Direct Loan Program.

## Types of Aid and Funding Limits
- **Direct Subsidized and Unsubsidized Loans**: Annual limits range from $5,500 to $20,500 for undergraduate and graduate students, depending on year in school, dependency status, and other factors.
- **Direct PLUS Loans**: Available to parents of dependent undergraduates and to graduate/professional students; loan amounts are determined by the cost of attendance minus other aid, as defined by federal law (the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”).
- Exact loan amounts for a given student cannot be determined from the source text.

## Application Process and Deadlines
1. Complete the FAFSA at fafsa.gov as early as possible. The FAFSA is available for any academic year that begins July 1 of the following year through June of the year after that.
2. List the foreign school’s Federal School Code on the FAFSA so the school can retrieve the data electronically.
3. Follow the foreign school’s specific instructions for loan paperwork, disbursement, and any additional deadlines they set.
4. First‑time borrowers must complete entrance counseling (online or in‑person) before receiving funds.
5. No separate FAFSA form exists for international study; the same form is used.

## Disbursement
- Loan funds are transferred electronically from the U.S. Treasury to the foreign school’s designated bank.
- The school applies funds to tuition, fees, and other charges first; any remaining balance is paid to the student.
- Disbursement may occur after the student has left the U.S., so travel costs must be covered independently.

## Repayment
- Repayment terms depend on whether the loan is subsidized, unsubsidized, or a PLUS loan.
- General repayment information is available on studentaid.gov under “Manage Loans.”

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- The source does not list which specific foreign schools currently participate; students must verify participation directly with the school.
- Exact loan limits for individual students (e.g., based on cost of attendance) are not provided.
- Deadlines for school‑specific paperwork are not detailed and vary by institution.
- Some data (e.g., medical‑school participation lists) are self‑reported by institutions and may be outdated.
- The source text is a government webpage and may be updated; the information reflects the content as of the retrieval date and should be cross‑checked with the latest official resources.

pages.title: International Graduate Admissions at UAB: Eligibility, Fees, and Deadlines
pages.focus_keyword: International Graduate Admissions at UAB: Eligibility, Fees, and Deadlines
pages.description: A concise guide to the key requirements and timelines for international students applying to graduate programs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB).
pages.content:
Eligibility
International applicants are citizens or permanent residents of a country other than the United States.  Applicants who are U.S. citizens but were born abroad must provide proof of U.S. citizenship (passport, birth‑abroad certificate, or naturalization certificate).  Those residing in the U.S. must upload current immigration documents (I‑20, DS‑2019, visa stamp, I‑94, I‑797, etc.).  Applicants applying from outside the U.S. or to online‑only programs are not required to submit immigration paperwork.

Academic Credentials
Applicants must demonstrate that they have earned the equivalent of a U.S. 4‑year bachelor’s degree.  Original transcripts and degree statements bearing an official stamp are required; unofficial copies may be submitted for review.  If the degree is not yet complete, a transcript showing at least 91 semester hours or six completed semesters is needed.

Transcript Evaluation
Foreign coursework must be evaluated on a course‑by‑course basis.  UAB offers an internal evaluation for a flat fee of $100, which covers all future graduate applications to UAB.  Alternatively, a NACES‑accredited evaluation may be submitted; UAB will accept any NACES member’s evaluation.

English Proficiency
Non‑English‑speaking applicants must submit scores that meet the Graduate School’s minimums: TOEFL 4.0, TOEFL Essentials 8.5, IELTS 6.5, PTEA 56, Duolingo 120 (programs may require higher scores).  Scores must be taken within the last two years.  Waivers are available for applicants who earned a U.S. degree with a GPA of 3.00 or higher or who are citizens of certain countries listed on the UAB website.

Application Process
1. Create an account on the UAB Graduate Online Application dashboard.
2. Complete the online application and upload required documents.
3. Pay the application fee ($50 for domestic, $60 for international; some programs may charge more).
4. Submit official test scores and recommendation letters electronically.
5. Review the application checklist in the dashboard to ensure all items are complete.

Fees
The standard application fee is $50 for domestic applicants and $60 for international applicants.  Certain programs may impose higher fees, which are assessed at the time of application.

Deadlines
Standard deadlines (unless a program specifies earlier dates):
• Fall 2026 – Application fee due by August 1, 2026; application submitted by August 17, 2026.
• Spring 2027 – Application fee due by December 1, 2026; application submitted by January 4, 2027.

Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) provides numerous scholarships and fellowships aimed at supporting both U.S. and international students. The availability of these funds can change each year, and the application process is closely tied to the admissions process.

To apply for HKS scholarships and fellowships, students must complete the HKS Financial Aid Application after submitting their application for admission. It's important to note that there are limited opportunities to apply for these funds after admission or enrollment.

HKS offers a wide range of scholarships and fellowships, including:
- **American Service Fellowship**: Full scholarship for U.S. public servants and military veterans.
- **Charles Edison Fund Fellowship**: For students extending the Science, Technology, and Public Policy Program.
- **Public Service Fellowships**: Cover tuition and fees for students committed to public service careers.
- **Middle East-North Africa Fellowship**: For students from specific regions such as Iraq's Kurdistan, Somaliland, Tunisia, and Yemen.

### Research Center Fellowships
Several scholarships are administered by HKS research centers, such as:
- **Ash Center for Democratic Governance and Innovation**: Supports students committed to strengthening democracy.
- **Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs**: Offers fellowships for students interested in science, technology, and international affairs.

### External Funding Opportunities
HKS students can also explore external funding options, including government sponsorships, partner organization scholarships, and other external scholarships from organizations like Fulbright and Rotary Clubs.

### Special Programs
- **Yellow Ribbon Program**: Provides additional financial assistance to veterans eligible for the Post-9/11 GI Bill.
- **Tuition Assistance Plan (TAP)**: Available for Harvard University employees enrolled part-time in the MC/MPA Program.

### Known Eligibility and Funding Details
Eligibility often requires demonstrated merit, financial need, or specific professional or regional backgrounds. Funding amounts and availability can vary annually.

Harvard Kennedy School's scholarships and fellowships provide significant financial support to students, enabling them to pursue their educational and professional goals. Prospective students should carefully review eligibility criteria and application processes to maximize their chances of receiving aid.

pages.content:
# Overview
The Graduate School at the University of Virginia encourages doctoral students to seek external funding to supplement their living support, reduce teaching duties, and potentially extend guaranteed support into a sixth year. Students are advised to obtain faculty and peer feedback before submitting applications. The Graduate School also co‑hosts grant‑writing workshops and provides access to discovery tools such as Pivot and GrantForward.

# Fellowships
## Jefferson Scholars Foundation Graduate Fellowships
- **Purpose**: Two‑year dissertation completion fellowship and postdoctoral appointment with the College Fellows.
- **Eligibility**: Top doctoral students in all arts and sciences fields.
- **Funding**: Not specified in the source.
- **Deadline**: Announced annually in December.

## Scholars’ Lab Fellowships in the Digital Humanities
- **Praxis Program**: Supports a team of six UVA PhD students to develop, publish, and promote a digital project over an academic year.
- **Digital Humanities Prototyping Fellowship**: For individual graduate students developing a specific project.
- **Digital Humanities Dissertation Fellowship**: For advanced doctoral students completing dissertations with digital content.
- **Eligibility, funding, and deadlines**: Not detailed in the source.

# Grants
## AHSS Summer Research Grants
- **Sponsor**: Graduate School of Arts and Sciences and Office of Graduate and Postdoctoral Affairs.
- **Purpose**: Stimulate preliminary dissertation research for students near the proposal stage.
- **Funding**: Up to $6,000 per award.
- **Eligibility**: PhD students in arts, humanities, or social sciences who are no more than three years into their program.
- **Deadline**: Monday, March 2, 2026.

# Exchange Fellowships
## A&S Exchange Fellowship: École Normale Supérieure (ENS) – Paris, France
- **Purpose**: Incremental year of financial support for advanced doctoral students in humanities and social sciences.
- **Funding**: $14,800 paid over the academic year plus $7,200 GSAS summer stipend.
- **Teaching Relief**: Two semesters.
- **Eligibility**: Advanced doctoral students who have completed candidacy requirements before the fellowship start.
- **Language Requirement**: Fluency in French.
- **Travel & Visa**: Student responsible for obtaining visa; ENS assists with formalities.
- **Deadline**: Applications due annually on November 1; awards announced by late December.
- **Application Materials**: Statement of purpose (max 2 pages), letter of support from dissertation advisor, confirmation of candidacy.

## A&S Exchange Fellowship: Technische Universität Dortmund – Dortmund, Germany
- **Purpose**: Incremental year of financial support for advanced doctoral students in humanities and social sciences.
- **Funding**: Teaching wages from TU Dortmund (€13,000 ≈ $14,800) plus a fellowship stipend of $14,000 from the Graduate School.
- **Teaching Requirement**: Design and teach two two‑hour courses per semester in English.
- **Eligibility**: Advanced doctoral students who have completed candidacy requirements before the fellowship start.
- **Language Requirement**: Knowledge of German helpful but not required.
- **Travel & Visa**: Student responsible for obtaining visa; TU Dortmund assists with formalities.
- **Deadline**: Applications due annually on February 1; awards announced in late March.
- **Contact**: Jeffrey Grossman (jg2t@virginia.edu).

# Dumas Malone Graduate Research Fellowship
- **Sponsor**: Thomas Jefferson Memorial Foundation, Inc.
- **Purpose**: Support research of advanced graduate students needing to investigate archives abroad.
- **Funding**: Not specified.
- **Deadline**: Monday, March 2, 2026.

# Albert Gallatin Graduate Research Fellowship
- **Sponsor**: Thomas Jefferson Memorial Foundation.
- **Purpose**: Support graduate students researching international affairs who require travel.
- **Funding**: Not specified.
- **Deadline**: Monday, March 2, 2026.

# Dean’s PhD‑Architecture Fellowships
- **Purpose**: Support students whose dissertation research benefits from a graduate certificate in Historic Preservation or Urban Design.
- **Eligibility**: Students in any Arts & Sciences doctoral program during their second or third years.
- **Benefits**: One semester of teaching relief, $2,000 additional living support for Urban Design certificate, full tuition payment for the Summer Design Institute.
- **Deadline**: Applications accepted from January 15 through March 1; awards announced in the first week of April.

# Known Eligibility, Funding, and Deadlines
- Eligibility criteria are explicitly stated for AHSS Summer Research Grants, ENS and TU Dortmund exchange fellowships, and Dean’s PhD‑Architecture Fellowships.
- Funding amounts are specified for AHSS Summer Research Grants ($6,000), ENS fellowship ($14,800 + $7,200 stipend), and TU Dortmund fellowship ($14,000 stipend + €13,000 teaching wages). Other fellowships list no funding amounts.
- Deadlines are provided for AHSS Summer Research Grants, ENS, TU Dortmund, Dumas Malone, Albert Gallatin, and Dean’s PhD‑Architecture Fellowships.

While some opportunities have clear eligibility, funding, and deadline details, others lack complete information. Students are encouraged to seek guidance from faculty, review the Graduate School’s resources, and verify details directly with the sponsoring offices before applying.

pages.content:
## Application Process Overview
The Office of Graduate Admissions accepts electronic applications for designated graduate degree and certificate programs. Applicants must submit all required materials online; hard‑copy documents are uploaded as instructed. Once submitted, the application is final and cannot be amended.

## Application Fee and Waiver
- Non‑refundable application fee: $90.
- Fee waivers are available for eligible applicants who meet specific criteria (see Eligibility for Fee Waiver). Waiver requests are processed in 1‑2 hours and applicants are notified by email.

## Eligibility for an Application Fee Waiver
Applicants may request a waiver if they belong to any of the following groups:
- Active duty or veteran military members (including those separated after April 1, 2024).
- Current or recent U.S. federal civil employees or contractors.
- Recent Georgetown undergraduate alumni (class of 2024‑2027).
- U.S. citizens with demonstrated financial need who meet categories such as Pell Grant recipients, GRE fee‑reduction recipients, or need‑based aid recipients.
- Participants in numerous external programs (e.g., Fulbright Scholars, McNair Scholars, LSAMP, etc.).
- Certain graduate programs may automatically waive the fee if the application is submitted by a program‑specific deadline (deadline not listed in the source).

## Required Application Materials
### Academic Statement of Purpose
- Approximately 500 words unless program‑specific guidance states otherwise.
- Should address intellectual interests, academic and professional goals, and proposed study topics.

### Optional Diversity/Personal Background Statement
- Up to 500 words describing how personal background or experiences will contribute to Georgetown’s community.

### Transcripts
- Upload unofficial copies of all undergraduate and graduate transcripts (≥15 credits or prerequisite courses).
- Official transcripts are required only after an admission offer is made.
- International transcripts should be accompanied by a WES/ICAP evaluation or other NACES‑member evaluation, and English translations if not in English.

### Recommendations
- Typically three official recommendations (some programs require two). Submitted via Georgetown’s online recommendation system.

### Standardized Test Scores
- Required tests vary by program (GRE, GRE Subject, GMAT, MCAT, etc.).
- Scores must be sent directly from the testing agency and received by the program’s application deadline.
- No unofficial score reports are accepted.

### English Proficiency
- Required for applicants whose prior degree was not taught in English.
- Minimum TOEFL iBT: 80 (old scale) or 100 (new scale) or 4/5 on the new scale (effective Jan 21 2026).
- Minimum IELTS: 7.0 or 7.5, depending on program.
- Scores must be sent directly to Georgetown (code 5244 for TOEFL/IELTS).

## Funding and Financial Aid
- International students may be eligible for institutional funds such as assistantships, fellowships, and scholarships, but are generally ineligible for U.S. federal loans.
- Specific scholarship programs are listed under fee‑waiver eligibility (e.g., Fulbright, Gates Millennium Scholars, etc.).
- Detailed funding amounts and eligibility criteria are program‑specific and not provided in the source.

## Deadlines and Timing
- The source does not specify a universal application deadline; deadlines are program‑specific.
- Some programs may have automatic fee‑waiver deadlines, but exact dates are not listed.
- Test scores should be taken at least one month before the program deadline.

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- Exact application deadlines for individual graduate programs are not included.
- Specific funding amounts, eligibility thresholds, and award types vary by department and are not detailed.
- Program‑specific requirements (e.g., additional essays, portfolios, or credential evaluations) are referenced but not enumerated.
- The source does not provide contact information for program‑level admissions officers.

## Additional Policies
- Applicants are responsible for ensuring all materials are received by the deadline.
- Forged or altered documents result in disqualification.
- Special Student Status may be offered to applicants who do not meet standard criteria, allowing limited graduate coursework without degree eligibility.
- Applicants with disabilities can request accommodations through the Academic Resource Center.

## Resources
- Application portal for status checks and document uploads.
- Georgetown’s Privacy Policy and GDPR notice for data handling.
- EducationUSA for international applicant guidance.

pages.content:
## Eligibility
- Must hold a completed and officially conferred U.S. four‑year bachelor’s degree from a regionally accredited U.S. institution, or an institutionally‑recognized international equivalent recognized by the foreign country’s Ministry of Higher Education.
- International applicants must meet the application deadlines set by their department and the I‑20 document deadlines.

## Application Process
- Submit an application through the University of Utah’s ApplyYourself system.
- Some programs require additional program‑specific applications; check the individual department page.
- Pay the non‑refundable graduate application fee of $65 (international applicants). Some departments may offer a fee waiver; consult the department’s website.
- The application will be evaluated only after all required fees and documents are received.

## Required Documents
- Copy of all college‑level transcripts (original and English translation if needed). Transcripts must include the student’s name, institution name, degrees conferred with dates, and a copy of the diploma if not listed.
- Proof of English proficiency, if required by the program.
- Official transcripts will be required after admission.
- SEVIS/I‑20 documents are requested only after admission and intent to enroll are confirmed.

## Fees and Funding
- Graduate application fee: $65 (international).
- International students must provide proof of funding for at least 9 credit hours per semester to obtain an I‑20.
- The University of Utah does not guarantee funding; students must secure their own financial support.

## Estimated Graduate Expenses (2026‑2027)
| Category | Master’s | Doctorate |
|---|---|---|
| Living Expenses (Housing & Food) | $19,198 | $19,198 |
| Books & Course Materials | $1,600 | $1,600 |

- Living costs may be higher if living off‑campus.
- International students pay non‑resident tuition rates; resident tuition may apply during the summer term.

## Tuition Waiver (House Bill 118)
- Eligible foreign nationals who attended a Utah high school for three or more years and graduated (or will graduate) may qualify for a tuition waiver that covers the non‑resident portion of tuition.

# Overview
Temple University provides a range of scholarships specifically for international students. The awards are merit‑based, creative‑prompt based, or tied to particular initiatives such as intercultural exchange or sister‑city partnerships. All scholarships are announced by April 1 each year, and students must meet the specified eligibility criteria and submit required materials by the stated deadlines.

# Merit Scholarships
- **Eligibility**: First‑year or transfer international students with strong academic records.
- **Funding**: Up to $20,000 per year for first‑year students (maximum of four years). Transfer students receive variable amounts.
- **Application**: No separate application; the admissions application is used for consideration.
- **Deadlines**: Submit all documentation and admissions application by the admissions deadline (exact date not specified in the source).

# #WhyUS Scholarship
- **Eligibility**: First‑year or transfer international applicants who have applied or are admitted to Temple.
- **Funding**: $2,000 to $10,000 per year for up to four consecutive years (first‑year) or two years (transfer).
- **Application**: Submit a creative response to the prompt via the #WhyUS application form. Formats include essay (≤250 words), video (≤1 min), audio, photo collage, meme, drawing, or painting. Non‑written submissions require a brief paragraph description.
- **Deadlines**: Application deadline March 1; winners announced April 1. Enrollment deposit deadline May 1.
- **Additional Notes**: Winners may combine this award with other scholarships and are expected to serve as #WhyUS ambassadors for up to 10 hrs per semester.

# #YouAreWelcomeHere Scholarship
- **Eligibility**: First‑year international applicants who demonstrate interest in intercultural learning and exchange.
- **Funding**: $20,000 per year, renewable annually.
- **Application**: Submit through the Common Application and the #YouAreWelcomeHere application with an essay or video by February 1.
- **Deadlines**: Application deadline February 1; winners announced April 1; enrollment deposit deadline May 1.

# Sister City Scholarships
- **Eligibility**: First‑year applicants from Philadelphia’s sister cities (e.g., Abruzzo, Italy; Aix‑en‑Provence, France; Douala, Cameroon; Florence, Italy; Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Incheon, Korea; Kobe, Japan; Nizhny Novgorod, Russia; Tel Aviv‑Yafo, Israel; Tianjin, China; Toruń, Poland).
- **Funding**: $10,000 per academic year for four years.
- **Application**: Complete the Sister City Scholarship application (details not provided in the source).
- **Deadlines**: Winners announced April 1.

# Application Process Summary
1. Apply for admission via the Common Application.
2. Submit the relevant scholarship application(s) (Merit, #WhyUS, #YouAreWelcomeHere, Sister City) by the specified deadlines.
3. Provide required materials (essays, videos, photos, etc.) in the accepted formats.
4. If awarded, claim the scholarship by submitting an enrollment deposit by May 1.

Overview
---
NYU Steinhardt awards millions of need‑ and merit‑based graduate scholarships each year. Most awards are reserved for full‑time, on‑campus U.S. citizens or permanent residents, though several programs target non‑U.S. citizens, service alumni, or part‑time students. Applicants must generally submit a FAFSA (by March 1 for Summer/Fall, November 1 for Spring) and meet program‑specific deadlines.

Eligibility
---
* **Steinhardt Graduate Scholarship** – Full‑time master’s, advanced certificate, or artist‑diploma students who are U.S. citizens/permanent residents; must demonstrate academic achievement and financial need. Automatic consideration when admission and FAFSA deadlines are met.
* **Cuppy Africa Steinhardt Scholars Stipend** – Two newly admitted full‑time on‑campus master’s/advanced‑certificate/diploma students starting Fall, who earned their bachelor’s degree in Africa. No separate eligibility beyond citizenship status (U.S. citizens/permanent residents) and full‑time enrollment.
* **Service‑Based Scholarships** – AmeriCorps Alumni, City Year members/alumni, Teach for America alumni, and Returned Peace Corps Volunteers. Require completion of service before the Fall semester start and full‑time enrollment.
* **NYU Peace Corps Coverdell Fellowship** – Returned Peace Corps Volunteers pursuing a full‑time on‑campus MA or MS. Provides 50 % tuition, health insurance, and leadership programming. Must answer “yes” on the admission application and submit required documents.
* **Global Citizen Scholarship** – Non‑U.S. citizens or non‑permanent residents (including visa and DACA applicants) with strong prior academic records. Competitive; full‑time on‑campus master’s/advanced‑certificate/diploma students.
* **Steinhardt Music Talent Scholarship** – Talent‑based awards for newly admitted fall‑semester master’s students in instrumental, jazz, vocal, or piano performance programs. Requires graduate application by Dec 1; no separate scholarship form.
* **Part‑Time Student Scholarships** – Centennial Scholarships (competitive, based on academic achievement) and Mayor’s Graduate Scholarship Program (up to five partial tuition awards for NYC employees). Automatic consideration when admission and FAFSA deadlines are met and part‑time status is indicated.
* **Online Student Scholarships** – Teacher Residency scholarships (details via contact email/phone). Specific eligibility not fully described in the source.
* **Teacher Education Scholarships** – Every newly admitted full‑time teacher‑education master’s student receives a scholarship: $20,000 for one‑year programs, $15,000 per year for two‑year programs. Requires admission application by Jan 15; no separate scholarship form.

Funding

* **Mayor’s Graduate Scholarship** – Partial tuition; precise amounts not indicated.

Deadlines

* **Steinhardt Graduate Scholarship** – Implicitly tied to FAFSA deadlines above.
* **Cuppy Africa Stipend** – March 1 for Fall semester start.

Introduction
The University of California, Riverside Graduate Division provides a curated list of external funding resources for graduate students. This article synthesizes that information, highlighting searchable databases, specific fellowship programs, eligibility criteria, award amounts, and known unknowns.

Major Funding Databases and Search Tools
- Fellowship Finder (UIUC Office of External Fellowships): over 1,100 grants searchable by field, citizenship, study stage, and award type.
- Foundation Center Online Directory: 140,000 U.S. foundations; free access via Inland Empire United Way (contact Alisa Lemke at ALemke@ieuw.org).
- Funding for Underrepresented Students (Affordable Colleges Online): graduate‑level opportunities for underrepresented groups.
- Funding for Undocumented Students (My Undocumented Life): regularly updated list for undocumented graduate students.
- GRAPES (UCLA): >500 private and public awards with advanced search filters.
- Grants.gov: discretionary funding from 26 U.S. agencies, primarily science and technology but includes other areas.
- Newton’s List: user‑driven international funding for natural and social sciences.
- NSF E‑Bulletin, NIH Guide, Pathways to Science, Pivot: additional searchable portals for U.S. federal opportunities.

Selected Fellowship Opportunities
Aga Khan Foundation: International Scholarship Programme
Eligibility: Nationals of Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Syria, Egypt, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Madagascar, Mozambique (or diaspora in France, Portugal, UK, USA, Canada); students from developing countries with no other financing; preference for under‑30 applicants; master’s level; must not have started studies.
Funding: Up to 2 years, 50 % fellowship / 50 % loan.
Deadline: Application period usually opens in January.

American Antiquarian Society: Hench Post‑Dissertation Fellowship
Eligibility: Scholars with a dissertation project aligned with the Society’s collections; demonstrated scholarly qualifications.
Funding: 12‑month stipend of $40,000.
Deadline: Applications usually due in October.

American Geophysical Union: Horton Research Grant
Eligibility: No citizenship requirement; topics in hydrology (physical, chemical, biological) or water‑resources policy (economics, systems analysis, sociology, law).
Funding: Up to $10,000 for one year.
Deadline: Application usually due in March.

Audio Engineering Society Educational Foundation: Graduate Students Grant
Eligibility: Worldwide graduate students who are AES members; must have completed at least one year of graduate study; tuition payments made directly to the graduate school.
Funding: Not specified in the source (N/A).
Deadline: Applications usually due in May.

Charles Babbage Institute: Adelle and Erwin Tomash Fellowship in the History of Information Technology
Eligibility: Doctoral students who have completed all requirements except dissertation research and writing.
Funding: $14,000 stipend.
Deadline: Applications usually open in Fall.

Christine Mirzayan Science & Technology Policy Graduate Fellowship Program
Eligibility: Early‑career professionals; full‑time 12‑week immersion at the National Academies; focus on science‑policy careers.
Funding: Not quantified in the source.
Deadline: Application period opens in June and closes in August; program runs March‑May.

Davis‑Putter Scholarship Fund
Eligibility: Students active in U.S. social and economic justice movements; preference for applicants planning to work in the United States.
Funding: Up to $15,000 per year (July 1 – June 30).
Deadline: Usually due in April.

Harry Frank Guggenheim Foundation: Emerging Scholar Awards
Eligibility: Graduate‑student researchers in the final year of a doctoral dissertation on any aspect of violence; any natural or social science discipline.
Funding: $25,000.
Deadline: Usually due in February.

Herb Society of America: Research Grant
Eligibility: Research on historical, scientific, or social uses of herbs (flavoring, medicine, ornament, economic, industrial, cosmetic).
Funding: Up to $10,000.
Deadline: Usually due in February.

Horowitz Foundation for Social Policy: Research Grants
Eligibility: Projects with a social‑policy application at global or local level; evaluated on feasibility, originality, methodology, etc.
Funding: Up to $10,000.
Deadline: Annually in the fall.

International Reading Association: Constance McCullough International Research Grant
Eligibility: Members of the International Literacy Association conducting research on reading problems abroad.
Funding: $2,000.
Deadline: Grant reopens August 2026.

International Reading Association: Steven A. Stahl Grant
Eligibility: Graduate students with at least three years of teaching experience conducting classroom research to improve reading instruction.
Funding: $1,000.
Deadline: Grant reopens August 2026.

International Reading Association: Jeanne S. Chall Research Fellowship
Eligibility: Doctoral students planning or beginning dissertations on reading; must be ILA members.
Funding: $5,000.
Deadline: Grant reopens August 2025.

P.E.O. International Peace Scholarship Fund
Eligibility: Women from countries other than the United States pursuing graduate study.
Funding: Up to $12,500.
Deadline: Usually due in December.

Unknowns and Source Limitations
- Many deadlines are described as “usually” and may shift; the source explicitly notes that information is not updated daily.
- Several programs (e.g., Audio Engineering Society, Mirzayan Fellowship) lack explicit award amounts in the source.
- Eligibility details may be incomplete; some listings mention citizenship or membership requirements without exhaustive criteria.
- URLs in the source are truncated or incomplete, requiring verification on official program websites.
- The compiled list is not exhaustive; additional external fellowships exist beyond those mentioned.

Conclusion
Graduate students can leverage a variety of searchable databases and targeted fellowship programs to secure external funding. Because the source material is not continuously updated and some details are missing, applicants should confirm eligibility, award amounts, and deadlines directly with each funding organization before applying.

pages.title: Month-by-Month Guide to Planning a Fully Funded PhD Abroad
pages.focus_keyword: Month-by-Month Guide to Planning a Fully Funded PhD Abroad
pages.description: A practical overview of the typical steps, eligibility requirements, funding options, and common deadlines for applying to PhD programmes overseas, with a critical look at the limitations of the Instagram source that inspired this guide.
pages.content:
## Introduction
The Instagram post by Ed Advisory offers a high‑level, month‑by‑month timeline for preparing a PhD application abroad. While the visual format is useful for motivation, it lacks detailed evidence, citations, and context. This article synthesises widely‑available information from university admissions offices, scholarship bodies, and government visa guidelines to provide an evidence‑based, yet cautious, roadmap.

## Typical Eligibility Criteria
- **Academic qualifications**: Most PhD programmes require a relevant bachelor's degree (often with honours) or a master's degree. Some fields accept a strong bachelor's degree alone, but this varies by discipline and country.
- **Grade point average (GPA) / class rank**: Competitive programmes often look for a GPA of 3.5/4.0 or equivalent. Exact thresholds differ between institutions.
- **English language proficiency**: For non‑native speakers, tests such as IELTS (usually ≥6.5 overall) or TOEFL iBT (≥90) are commonly required.
- **Standardised tests**: Certain countries (e.g., the US) may still request GRE scores, though many programmes have moved away from this requirement.
- **Research experience**: Prior research, publications, or a strong research proposal are critical for funding decisions.

## Funding Landscape
- **University‑provided scholarships**: Many universities offer fully funded PhD positions that include tuition waivers and a stipend. These are often advertised on departmental webpages.
- **National and international fellowships**: Examples include the Fulbright Program (USA), DAAD (Germany), Chevening (UK), and Erasmus Mundus (EU). Eligibility criteria and award amounts vary.
- **Research council grants**: In the UK, the UKRI funds PhDs through Doctoral Training Partnerships; in Canada, the NSERC provides scholarships.
- **Industry‑sponsored projects**: Some PhD positions are tied to specific research projects funded by corporations.
- **Funding timelines**: Scholarship applications frequently close between November and February for programmes starting the following autumn.

## Typical Application Timeline (Month‑by‑Month)
| Month | Typical Activities |
|-------|--------------------|
| **Jan‑Feb** | Identify target universities and supervisors; review programme requirements; create a spreadsheet of deadlines. |
| **Mar‑Apr** | Prepare or update CV, personal statement, and research proposal; register for language tests if needed; request transcripts. |
| **May‑Jun** | Reach out to potential supervisors with a concise email and draft proposal; seek feedback on research ideas. |
| **Jul‑Aug** | Refine research proposal based on supervisor input; begin writing scholarship essays; secure letters of recommendation. |
| **Sep‑Oct** | Submit formal applications (often through university portals) and scholarship applications; pay any application fees. |
| **Nov‑Dec** | Follow up with departments; prepare for possible interviews (virtual or in‑person). |
| **Jan‑Feb** | Receive admission decisions; evaluate funding offers; negotiate if multiple offers exist. |
| **Mar‑Apr** | Accept offer, arrange visa paperwork, and secure housing. |
| **May‑Jun** | Finalise travel plans and enrolment; attend orientation sessions. |

*Note*: Exact months shift depending on the academic calendar of the host country (e.g., US programmes often start in August/September, while many European programmes begin in October).

## Key Unknowns and Risks
- **Specific programme deadlines**: Universities set their own dates; some have rolling admissions, others strict cut‑offs.
- **Funding availability**: Not all applicants receive full funding; competition is high and criteria differ across scholarships.
- **Visa processing times**: These can vary widely and may be impacted by geopolitical events.
- **Supervisor responsiveness**: Early contact does not guarantee a supervisor’s willingness to take on a new student.

## Limitations of the Source Material
- The Instagram reel provides a generic timeline without citations, making it impossible to verify the accuracy of the month ranges for any particular country or discipline.
- It promotes a consulting service (DM for guidance), which may introduce bias toward encouraging early contact with the service rather than independent research.
- No concrete data on success rates, funding amounts, or eligibility thresholds are presented.
- Visual content (images and videos) is not accessible in text form, limiting the ability to extract detailed information.

## Conclusion
While the month‑by‑month structure from the Instagram post can serve as a motivational scaffold, prospective PhD candidates should verify each step against official university and scholarship sources. Early planning, clear documentation of eligibility, and awareness of unknown variables are essential for securing a fully funded PhD position abroad.

pages.title: How to Apply to Graduate School at CUNY: Steps, Eligibility, Funding, and Deadlines
pages.focus_keyword: How to Apply to Graduate School at CUNY: Steps, Eligibility, Funding, and Deadlines
pages.description: A concise guide to the CUNY graduate application process, covering eligibility, required documents, funding options, typical deadlines, and the limits of the available source information.
pages.content:
Overview
CUNY offers graduate programs across its 15 colleges. Prospective students are encouraged to explore programs early, attend information sessions, and follow a series of documented steps before submitting an application.

Eligibility
The source does not list a single set of eligibility criteria for all programs. In general, applicants must have completed an undergraduate degree and meet any program‑specific GPA or prerequisite coursework requirements. Minimum GPA is often cited as 3.0, but this can vary. International students must provide English proficiency test scores (TOEFL, IELTS, or PTE) and may need document translation.

Application Steps
1. Identify programs of interest using the CUNY graduate program search.
2. Attend an information session or open house.
3. Review admission requirements and deadlines for each program.
4. Request official transcripts from all previously attended colleges.
5. Secure 2‑3 letters of recommendation, ideally from academic or professional contacts.
6. Prepare and submit any required standardized test scores (GRE, GMAT, LSAT, etc.).
7. For international applicants, arrange external evaluation or translation of documents, which can take several months.
8. Draft a personal statement and other essays, beginning at least three months before the deadline.
9. Complete the online application and submit all supporting materials.

Standardized Tests
Required tests differ by program. Common exams include GRE, GMAT, LSAT, NYS Teacher Certification tests, and TOEFL for non‑native English speakers. Applicants should schedule tests five to six months before the application deadline to allow time for score reporting and possible retakes.

Personal Statement
Programs may ask specific questions or provide open prompts. Writing should begin three months prior to submission to allow for feedback and revision.

Letters of Recommendation
Two or more letters are typically required. Applicants should contact potential recommenders at least one month before the deadline and provide them with a personal statement draft for context.

Transcripts
Official transcripts must be sent directly from each institution’s registrar. Some programs may require a minimum GPA of 3.0 and specific prerequisite courses. Non‑degree coursework can be used to satisfy prerequisites but does not count toward the graduate degree.

Funding and Financial Aid
CUNY’s Office of Financial Aid recommends filing the FAFSA before applying. Funding (scholarships, grants, loans, work‑study) is allocated on a first‑come, first‑served basis. Detailed information about specific graduate funding sources is available on the “Financing Your Graduate Education” page, but the source does not list amounts or eligibility criteria.

Deadlines
Deadlines vary by college and program. Applicants should consult each department’s deadline page and create a personal calendar. Standardized test scores, recommendation letters, transcripts, and financial‑aid applications should be timed to meet the earliest program deadline.

Unknowns and Source Limitations
- Exact GPA thresholds, prerequisite courses, and test score requirements are program‑specific and not detailed in the source.
- Specific scholarship amounts, eligibility rules, and application procedures are not provided.
- Precise application deadlines for individual programs are not listed; only a general statement that they vary.
- The source does not include data on acceptance rates, average applicant profiles, or post‑acceptance steps.
- All information reflects what is publicly posted on the CUNY graduate admissions page as of the retrieval date and may change without notice.

Conclusion
Prospective CUNY graduate students should start planning early, verify program‑specific requirements, and monitor deadlines closely. While the source outlines a clear procedural framework, many details remain program‑dependent and require direct confirmation from the relevant CUNY college.

pages.title: Applying to Graduate School: Key Steps, Eligibility, Funding, and Timeline
pages.focus_keyword: Applying to Graduate School: Key Steps, Eligibility, Funding, and Timeline
pages.description: A concise, evidence‑based overview of the graduate‑school application process, covering typical timelines, eligibility factors, funding options, and the uncertainties that applicants should verify with individual programs.
pages.content:
## Introduction
Applying to graduate school involves multiple coordinated steps, from early planning to final enrollment decisions. The information below synthesizes guidance from a Kaplan Test Prep guide (April 2021) while noting where the source does not provide specifics.

## Known Eligibility Factors
- **Academic Record**: Most programs require a cumulative undergraduate GPA and, for some, a major‑specific GPA.
- **Standardized Tests**: The GRE is commonly required; programs may publish minimum scores or average admitted scores, but these details vary and are not listed in the source.
- **Letters of Recommendation**: Typically two or three letters from professors or professional supervisors.
- **Personal Statement**: A written essay describing goals, fit, and experiences.
- **Interview**: Some programs require an interview, either with admissions staff or alumni.
- **Program‑Specific Requirements**: Certain fields may need prerequisite coursework, portfolios, or additional tests (e.g., LSAT for law, MCAT for medicine). The guide advises checking each program’s website.

## General Application Timeline
| Approx. Time Before Start | Recommended Actions |
|---------------------------|---------------------|
| **2 years** | Research fields, list potential programs, talk to advisors, attend open houses. |
| **1 year** | Register for the GRE, begin test preparation (minimum 3 months), start FAFSA, identify funding sources, request recommendation letters early. |
| **9 months** | Application portals typically open; submit applications as early as possible. |
| **6 months** | Receive decisions, compare offers, consider financial aid packages, and make enrollment choice. |

The guide emphasizes that most programs open applications about nine months before the intended start date and that deadlines generally fall in the fall or winter of the preceding year.

## Funding Options Mentioned
- **Federal Aid**: FAFSA (no parental information required for graduate students) unlocks federal loans, grants, and work‑study.
- **Merit‑Based Aid**: Scholarships, fellowships, teaching or research assistantships (often include tuition remission and stipends).
- **External Scholarships**: Fastweb.com listings, Fulbright, Marshall, Rhodes scholarships (specific to certain fields or destinations).
- **Military Benefits**: Post‑9/11 GI Bill (covers tuition at public schools, up to ~US$22,000/year at private schools) and Yellow Ribbon programs.
- **Employer Assistance**: Tuition reimbursement programs, sometimes contingent on continued employment.
- **Faith‑Based and Non‑Traditional Scholarships**: Targeted awards for specific demographics or age groups.
- **Personal Financing**: IRA loans, home‑equity loans, or personal savings (not recommended without careful consideration).

## Known Deadlines and Application Windows
- **GRE Test Dates**: Offered nearly daily at most centers; schedule at least three months before the intended test date.
- **FAFSA**: Opens January 1 each year; early submission is advised because many aid programs are first‑come, first‑served.
- **Program Deadlines**: Vary by institution; the guide suggests checking each school’s website for exact dates.

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- **Exact GRE Score Requirements**: The guide does not list specific score thresholds for any program.
- **Program‑Specific Funding Amounts**: No data on stipend sizes, tuition coverage percentages, or scholarship award amounts.
- **Currentness**: The source was published in April 2021; policies, deadlines, and funding opportunities may have changed.
- **Variability Across Disciplines**: Some fields (e.g., clinical psychology) have state‑specific licensing requirements not detailed in the guide.
- **International Applicants**: No information on visa‑related eligibility or funding for non‑U.S. residents.

## Practical Tips for Applicants
1. **Start Early**: Begin research and networking at least two years before intended enrollment.
2. **Create a Master Calendar**: Track GRE registration, test dates, FAFSA submission, recommendation letter deadlines, and each program’s application deadline.
3. **Tailor Materials**: Customize personal statements and CVs to align with each program’s mission and faculty interests.
4. **Secure Recommendations**: Ask potential recommenders as soon as you decide to apply and provide them with clear deadlines and supporting documents.
5. **Financial Planning**: Complete FAFSA early, then explore merit‑based aid, employer benefits, and external scholarships.
6. **Verify Information**: Contact admissions offices directly for up‑to‑date GRE expectations, funding packages, and any program‑specific eligibility criteria.

## Conclusion
The graduate‑school application process is multi‑stage, requiring careful timing, documentation, and financial planning. While the Kaplan guide provides a solid framework, applicants must confirm details—especially eligibility thresholds, funding amounts, and exact deadlines—with each target institution to ensure a complete and competitive application.

pages.description: This evidence‑based overview summarizes key points about graduate‑level scholarships, including eligibility categories, funding coverage, typical deadlines, and practical advice for searching and applying. It also highlights known limitations of the source material and areas where information is uncertain.
pages.content:
## Introduction

Graduate‑level education can be costly.  According to the source, the average undergraduate tuition and fees in the United States were $19,749 in 2021 (NCES).  Scholarships are one of several financial‑aid options that can reduce this burden.

## Scholarship Eligibility Categories

The source lists four broad eligibility bases:

- **Need‑based** – awarded when a student demonstrates financial need.  The article notes that many need‑based scholarships require submission of the FAFSA.
- **Merit‑based** – awarded for academic or other achievements.  High GPA is often cited as a key criterion.
- **Diversity / Under‑represented Groups** – targeted at students from specific demographic or professional backgrounds.
- **Program‑specific** – tied to a particular graduate program or institution.

Other categories mentioned include professional‑association scholarships and employer‑funded awards.

## Funding Coverage

The article states that scholarships can cover either the entire tuition or a portion of it.  No specific dollar amounts or award limits are provided in the source.

## Typical Scholarship Sources

The source identifies several avenues for locating scholarships:

- **Financial Aid Offices** – university or college offices that manage institutional awards.
- **Online Scholarship Databases** – searchable platforms that list opportunities.
- **Professional Associations** – societies related to a student’s field of study.
- **Employers** – especially for employees seeking graduate education.
- **State Grant Agencies** – state‑level bodies that may offer awards.
- **Professional and Diversity Organizations** – groups that focus on under‑represented populations.

The article advises against paying for scholarship information, warning that such requests may signal scams.

## Application Strategy

Key recommendations from the source include:

- **Apply Early** – some scholarships have deadlines as early as a year before the anticipated start of the graduate program.
- **Tailor Your Application** – follow each scholarship’s specific instructions, especially regarding essay topics.
- **Highlight Achievements** – include academic performance, extracurricular involvement, and relevant work or volunteer experience.
- **Seek Feedback** – review application materials with mentors or advisors.
- **Maintain Strong Relationships** – cultivate connections with professors or supervisors who can provide letters of recommendation.

## Practical Tips for Searching

1. **Start Early** – begin research over a year before the intended program start date.
2. **Use Multiple Channels** – consult the financial aid office, online databases, professional associations, and employer resources.
3. **Verify Eligibility** – for need‑based awards, the FAFSA is typically required.
4. **Apply to Multiple Awards** – the source recommends applying to as many scholarships as possible.
5. **Avoid Scams** – do not pay for scholarship information; legitimate awards do not require a fee.

## FAQs Summary

- *How to know if I qualify for need‑based scholarships?* – Submit the FAFSA and follow the specific scholarship instructions.
- *Can I apply for multiple scholarships?* – Yes, applying to several is encouraged.
- *What to include in an essay?* – Varies by scholarship; follow the provided prompts.
- *When to start searching?* – Begin at least a year before the program start date.

## Known Eligibility, Funding, Deadline, Unknowns, and Source Limitations

### Known Eligibility
- Need‑based
- Merit‑based
- Diversity / Under‑represented groups
- Program‑specific
- Professional association
- Employer‑funded

### Funding Coverage
- Scholarships may cover the entire tuition or a portion of it.

### Typical Deadlines
- Some scholarships have deadlines as early as one year before the anticipated program start.

### Unknowns
- Exact number of available scholarships for graduate students.
- Specific award amounts for each category.
- Detailed eligibility criteria beyond those broadly described.
- Individual scholarship deadlines and application windows.

### Source Limitations
- The information originates from a single, unverified article.
- No direct verification of the claims (e.g., cost figures, scholarship details).
- Potentially outdated data (average cost figure is from 2021).
- No guarantee that the listed categories or advice apply to all institutions or regions.
- The article does not provide direct links to specific scholarship opportunities.

## Conclusion

Graduate‑level scholarships can make post‑baccalaureate education more affordable, but applicants must carefully assess eligibility, funding scope, and deadlines.  The source material offers a useful framework, yet its claims remain unverified and may lack completeness.  Prospective students should corroborate details with official institutional or organizational resources before making decisions.

pages.title: Financial Aid Options for International Students in the United States
pages.focus_keyword: Financial Aid Options for International Students in the United States
pages.description: A concise guide to what funding sources are available to F‑1 and J‑1 students, including university aid, private scholarships, no‑cosigner loans, work opportunities, and sponsor programs, with known eligibility rules, typical deadlines, and key uncertainties.
pages.content:
## Eligibility
- Federal student aid (FAFSA, Pell Grants, Direct Loans, Work‑Study) is generally **not available** to students on standard F‑1 or J‑1 visas. Exceptions exist for green‑card holders, refugees, asylees, and a few other protected categories, but most international applicants must look elsewhere.
- University need‑based aid is accessed through the **CSS Profile** (College Board) or school‑specific international aid forms. The CSS Profile costs **$25** for the first school and **$16** for each additional school; fee waivers for domestic students do not apply to international filers.
- Some private scholarships explicitly allow international applicants; eligibility varies by award and often includes visa status, academic record, and field of study.
- No‑cosigner loans are offered by a limited number of lenders (e.g., MPOWER Financing for under‑grad and graduate students, Prodigy Finance for graduate students). Eligibility depends on school participation and the applicant’s future earning potential.
- Work authorization is limited: on‑campus employment up to **20 hours/week** during term, full‑time during breaks; **CPT** (Curricular Practical Training) and **OPT** (Optional Practical Training) require school and USCIS approval, with OPT limited to **12 months** (extendable by **24 months** for STEM fields).

## Funding Sources
1. **Family Resources** – Personal or family savings remain the primary source.
2. **University Aid**
   - *Need‑blind & full‑need* schools (as of 2025‑2026): Harvard, Yale, Princeton, MIT, Amherst, Bowdoin, Dartmouth, Brown. These institutions do not consider financial need in admission and commit to meeting demonstrated need, typically with grants.
   - *Need‑aware* schools consider financial need during admission; requesting large aid packages may affect admission chances.
   - *Merit scholarships* (often automatic) are common at many public universities (e.g., University of Alabama) based on GPA and test scores.
3. **Private Scholarships & Sponsor Programs**
   - Organizations such as **Fulbright Foreign Student Program** (U.S. Department of State) fund graduate study and research; applications are submitted through home‑country commissions or U.S. embassies.
   - National governments may offer scholarships for citizens studying abroad; deadlines follow each country’s calendar.
   - Directories like **ScholarshipOwl** aggregate awards that accept international students.
4. **No‑Cosigner Loans**
   - **MPOWER Financing**: up to **$100,000**, fixed rate, available to eligible schools in the U.S. and Canada.
   - **Prodigy Finance**: graduate‑level loans, variable rate, limited to participating programs.
   - Traditional U.S. lenders (Sallie Mae, College Ave, Ascent, SoFi) require a U.S. cosigner.
5. **Employment**
   - On‑campus jobs for living expenses.
   - CPT and OPT for field‑related work (subject to authorization).
   - Graduate teaching/research assistantships that provide stipends and tuition waivers.

## Typical Deadlines
- **CSS Profile / school aid forms**: often due **before or with the admission deadline**; missing them can forfeit need‑based aid for the first year.
- **University merit scholarship grids**: align with admission cycles (usually **Nov‑Jan** for fall intake).
- **Fulbright and government scholarships**: vary by country; many close **6‑12 months** before the intended start term.
- **Loan applications**: should be completed after admission offers are received and before tuition payment deadlines (typically **May‑July** for fall semester).

## Unknowns & Source Limitations
- Exact tuition, housing, and living‑cost figures differ by institution and location; the source provides only a general $80,000 + figure for private universities.
- Current interest rates for MPOWER and Prodigy loans are described as “fixed” or “variable” but the precise percentages are not listed and can change over time.
- The list of need‑blind, full‑need schools may evolve after the 2025‑2026 cycle; readers must verify each school’s latest policy.
- Private scholarship amounts, eligibility criteria, and application windows are not detailed in the source; prospective applicants should consult each award’s official page.
- Visa work‑authorization rules (CPT/OPT) are subject to USCIS policy updates; the source’s description reflects the rules as of its last update (Sept 2026).
- The source mentions a “free AI prompt” and “personal funding checklist” but provides no verifiable link; these tools are not included.

## Practical Step‑by‑Step Plan
1. **Budget** the total cost of attendance, including tuition, fees, housing, and living expenses.
2. **Confirm ineligibility** for federal aid (FAFSA) unless holding a protected status.
3. **Identify target schools** – separate need‑blind/full‑need institutions from need‑aware and merit‑focused public universities.
4. **Prepare and submit** CSS Profile or school‑specific aid forms by each school’s deadline.
5. **Apply for merit scholarships** (automatic where available) during the admission cycle.
6. **Research sponsor/government scholarships** (e.g., Fulbright) early, respecting their independent timelines.
7. **Secure a no‑cosigner loan** only after exhausting grants and scholarships, if a funding gap remains.
8. **Plan for on‑campus work, CPT, or OPT** to cover living costs, not tuition.

## Common Pitfalls to Avoid
- Assuming FAFSA eligibility and filing it.
- Assuming all universities provide international aid.
- Overlooking the need‑aware impact on admission chances.
- Missing aid‑application deadlines, especially for the first year.
- Underestimating proof‑of‑funds requirements for the I‑20 visa document.
- Relying solely on work income to cover tuition.

By following this structured approach and verifying each piece of information with official university, lender, and government sources, international students can create a realistic financing plan for studying in the United States.

This article summarizes the available aid, eligibility criteria, payment schedules, and known gaps in the information.
pages.content:
## Overview
George Washington University (GW) provides merit‑based financial aid to international undergraduate applicants. GW does not offer need‑based or U.S. government aid to international students. All aid is awarded automatically during the application review unless a separate application is required.

## Merit Scholarships
- GW automatically considers all international applicants for merit scholarships.
- Students may qualify for more than one merit award, but only one scholarship can be granted.
- Scholarships are awarded only to students who do not receive GW employee benefits.
- For first‑year students, a scholarship can continue for up to 10 consecutive semesters, provided the student maintains full‑time enrollment and satisfactory academic progress.
- Scholarship funds can be used only toward undergraduate tuition expenses.
- The monetary value of each merit scholarship varies and is specified in the admission offer.

## Presidential Academic Scholarships
- First‑year fall applicants with strong academic credentials are automatically considered.
- The scholarship amount varies.
- Recipients are notified in their admission letter.

## You Are Welcome Here Scholarship
- GW offers two full‑tuition scholarships each year to first‑year fall applicants.
- Applicants must submit an essay or video that outlines how they will promote intercultural learning on campus.
- A CSS Profile (School Code 5246) is required.
- Eligibility: attended or graduated from a secondary school outside the United States and demonstrated interest and initiative in intercultural activities.
- Application is submitted through the admissions portal after the main application is received.
- Deadline for the scholarship application: January 31.
- If the scholarship application is not visible in the portal, applicants should email intadm@gwu.edu.

## UWC Scholars Partnership
- GW partners with the Davis United World College (UWC) Scholars program.
- UWC graduates admitted to GW may receive need‑based scholarships that can cover up to full tuition and fees.
- A CSS Profile is required for consideration.
- Scholarship amounts vary based on the applicant’s financial need.

## Financial Documentation Requirements
- U.S. law requires international students to submit documents proving the ability to pay for one year of study before visa documents are issued.
- Acceptable documents include a bank statement, certificate of deposit, scholarship or sponsorship award letter, or a combination.
- Funds may be in any currency, provided the amount equals the published cost of attendance.
- Documents must be in English or accompanied by an official English translation.
- Detailed instructions are available on GW’s International Applicant webpage.

## Tuition and Fees Payment
- Tuition, fees, and housing charges are due on the first day of each semester.
- All charges must be paid in full by the specified deadline.
- The published cost of attendance covers a nine‑month academic year (late August to early May).
- Married students or those bringing families should budget an additional $10,796 per year for a spouse and $5,394 per year for each child.
- Housing cost information is provided by GW’s Campus Living and Residential Education office.

## Eligibility and Restrictions
- International students are eligible for merit scholarships but not for need‑based or U.S. government aid.
- Students receiving GW employee benefits are ineligible for scholarships.
- Only one scholarship can be awarded per student.
- Scholarship funds are restricted to tuition and cannot be used for other expenses.

## Deadlines
- You Are Welcome Here Scholarship application: January 31.
- Other merit scholarships are considered automatically during the application review; no separate deadline is specified.
- Tuition and fee payments are due on the first day of each semester.

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- The exact monetary values of the merit, Presidential Academic, and UWC scholarships are not disclosed.
- Specific criteria for “strong academic credentials” for the Presidential Academic Scholarship are not detailed.
- The process for submitting the CSS Profile and the exact deadlines for that submission are not fully described.
- Information is drawn from a single university webpage; external verification or updates may not be reflected.
- No external links or additional resources are provided in the source text.

## Key Takeaways
- GW offers merit‑based aid to international undergraduates, with specific scholarships such as the Presidential Academic and You Are Welcome Here awards.
- Proof of financial capacity is mandatory for visa issuance.
- Scholarship applications have a clear deadline (January 31 for the You Are Welcome Here Scholarship), while other scholarships are awarded automatically.
- Applicants should review the International Applicant webpage for the most current details and contact GW admissions if questions arise.

pages.description: A concise guide to typical deadlines, eligibility requirements, funding options, and the uncertainties that applicants face when applying to U.S. graduate programs.
pages.content:
Introduction
Graduate‑school admissions in the United States are organized around a few recurring application cycles.  Most programs accept applications for fall admission (the most common entry point) and, in some cases, for spring or summer admission.  Because the information below is drawn from general patterns observed across many institutions, it should be used as a starting point rather than a definitive timetable.

Typical Application Cycles
Fall Admission
• Early‑Decision or Early‑Action: December–January
• Regular Decision: January–March
• Late Decision (if offered): April–May
Spring Admission
• Early‑Decision or Early‑Action: September–October
• Regular Decision: October–December
Summer Admission
• Early‑Decision or Early‑Action: May–June
• Regular Decision: June–August

Common Deadline Dates
The following dates are illustrative of the most common windows:
• Early‑Decision/Early‑Action: mid‑December to early‑January
• Regular Decision: late January to early‑March
• Late Decision (if available): late March to early‑May
These windows can shift by a week or two depending on the university, the specific department, and whether the program is a research or professional track.

Eligibility Criteria
While each program sets its own standards, the following elements are frequently required:
• A completed bachelor’s degree (or equivalent) from an accredited institution
• Official transcripts from all post‑secondary institutions attended
• Standardized test scores (GRE, GMAT, LSAT, MCAT, etc.) – many programs are test‑optional, but scores can strengthen an application
• Proof of English proficiency (TOEFL, IELTS, or equivalent) for non‑native speakers
• Letters of recommendation (usually 2–3)
• A statement of purpose or personal statement
• A resume or curriculum vitae
• Application fee (often waived for certain applicants)

Funding Opportunities
Graduate‑level funding in the U.S. typically comes from:
• Teaching or research assistantships (TAs/RA) that provide a stipend and tuition waiver
• Fellowships and scholarships offered by the university, department, or external foundations
• Grants or fellowships tied to specific research projects or demographic groups
• External funding from government agencies, industry partners, or professional societies
Applicants should identify funding options early, as many assistantships and fellowships have separate deadlines that may precede the general application deadline.

Uncertainties and Unknowns
• Program‑specific deadlines: Some departments set earlier or later dates than the general cycle.
• Early‑Decision/Early‑Action availability: Not all programs offer these options.
• Funding deadlines: Assistantship and fellowship deadlines can vary widely and may be earlier than the application deadline.
• Changes due to extraordinary circumstances (e.g., pandemic‑related adjustments) can alter deadlines.

Source Limitations
The information above is based on common practices observed across U.S. graduate programs.  It is not derived from a single authoritative source and should not replace direct consultation of individual university or department websites.  The Facebook post that prompted this article is an unverified community discussion and does not provide official deadlines or eligibility details.

Practical Tips
1. Create a spreadsheet to track each program’s application and funding deadlines.
2. Contact program coordinators early to confirm dates and clarify any special requirements.
3. Prepare application materials well in advance to avoid last‑minute issues.
4. Keep copies of all submitted documents and confirm receipt with the admissions office.
5. If funding is a concern, prioritize programs that offer assistantships or fellowships.

By approaching the application process systematically and verifying dates directly with each institution, applicants can reduce uncertainty and increase their chances of a successful admission.
